questions.stem: A 34-year-old bilateral lung recipient currently on tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day is developing a progressive cough and dyspnea. He reports that 5 months ago he had “the flu” and since then has been unable to get rid of the coughing spells. His dyspnea is getting worse, and the symptoms are unabating. A CT of the chest shows hyperinflation and patchy areas of inflammation. Bronchoscopy is unrevealing except for few gram-negative bacteria. What is the best course of action?
questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old bilateral lung recipient currently on tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day is developing a progressive cough and dyspnea. He reports that 5 months ago he had “the flu” and since then has been unable to get rid of the coughing spells. His dyspnea is getting worse, and the symptoms are unabating. A CT of the chest shows hyperinflation and patchy areas of inflammation. Bronchoscopy is unrevealing except for few gram-negative bacteria. What is the best course of action?

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the steroid dose in conjunction with Atrovent and albuterol

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Start azithromycin: This patient has symptoms of obliterative bronchiolitis. In the absence of histopathology, this is known as bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS). Approximately 7-15% of transplant recipients will develop this complication that likely represents a late form of rejection. The gradual, unrelenting, and sustained increase in symptoms is typical. CT shows hyperinflation and some patchy infiltrate. Treatments include modification of the immunosuppressive regimen or addition of azithromycin. Tacrolimus and mycophenolate are specifically recommended in this situation. Since this patient is already on tacrolimus, azithromycin is a reasonable addition. Azithromycin, through an immunomodulatory mechanism, has been shown to increase the FEV1 in patients with BOS by 41% and should be administered to this patient in a dose of 250 mg daily for 5 days, followed by 250 mg 3 times weekly. Preliminary reports suggest that prolonged oral azithromycin therapy may stop or reverse the decline in pulmonary function associated with BOS in some patients. Incorrect Options: Option A - Increase the dose of tacrolimus: Guidelines support the initiation of azithromycin. Option B - Start piperacillin/tazobactam and inhaled tobramycin: A minimal cough and lack of CT findings are contraindicative of pneumonia, even in the presence of few gram-negative bacteria; these usually represent colonization. Option D - Increase the steroid dose in conjunction with Atrovent and albuterol: Asthma is related to the episodic nature of symptoms. Although increased steroids will improve immunosuppression, inhalers will have minimal impact on the disease progression. @Neet_pg_bot

Incorrect Options:

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man presents complaining of pain and a crawling sensation in his legs. These symptoms have been worsening over the past few months. The patient has a history of coronary artery disease, hyperlipidemia and hypertension. His current medications are metformin, lisinopril, aspirin, atorvastatin, and a multivitamin. These sensations occur in both legs, usually at night before bed with a "cramping pain." The patient often has to get up and walk around for relief. He is frustrated that this sensation prevents him from getting to sleep at night. Vitals are within normal limits. Heart, lung, and abdomen findings are also within normal limits. On neurological exam, he is alerted and oriented, with a normal cranial nerve exam, 5/5 motor strength in all extremities, and intact sensation to all sensory modalities. His extremities are pertinent for smooth skin with minimal hair over the shins. Peripheral pulses are all normal. The patient has no edema or pain on palpation. A lab work-up reveals the following: hemoglobin 11 g/dl, MCV 75fL, HgbA1c 4.7%, vitamin B12 625ng/dL, folate 12ng/mL, methylmalonic acid normal, homocysteine within normal limits, 25-hydroxy vitamin D 100 nmol/L, ferritin 40 mcg/L. Replacing which of the following might relieve his symptoms?
questions.stemHtml:
A 52-year-old man presents complaining of pain and a crawling sensation in his legs. These symptoms have been worsening over the past few months. The patient has a history of coronary artery disease, hyperlipidemia and hypertension. His current medications are metformin, lisinopril, aspirin, atorvastatin, and a multivitamin. These sensations occur in both legs, usually at night before bed with a "cramping pain." The patient often has to get up and walk around for relief. He is frustrated that this sensation prevents him from getting to sleep at night. Vitals are within normal limits. Heart, lung, and abdomen findings are also within normal limits.
On neurological exam, he is alerted and oriented, with a normal cranial nerve exam, 5/5 motor strength in all extremities, and intact sensation to all sensory modalities. His extremities are pertinent for smooth skin with minimal hair over the shins. Peripheral pulses are all normal. The patient has no edema or pain on palpation. A lab work-up reveals the following: hemoglobin 11 g/dl, MCV 75fL, HgbA1c 4.7%, vitamin B12 625ng/dL, folate 12ng/mL, methylmalonic acid normal, homocysteine within normal limits, 25-hydroxy vitamin D 100 nmol/L, ferritin 40 mcg/L.
Replacing which of the following might relieve his symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Iron: This patient has restless legs syndrome (RLS) which is associated with iron deficiency. A serum ferritin concentration lower than 45 to 50 mcg/L has been associated with an increased severity of RLS, and iron replacement is recommended if the fasting serum ferritin level is ≤75 mcg/L. The 4 major criteria of the RLS diagnosis include the following: (1) Symptoms are worse at night and decreased or absent during the day. (2) Sensation, including pain or paresthesia, results in a strong urge to move. (3) Sensation begins with rest or relaxation, often when laying down for bed. (4) Sensation is improved or relieved with movement. This patient is exhibiting all of these symptoms, making RLS the most likely diagnosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Insulin: This patient does not have diabetes mellitus, given his normal HgBA1C, and he is therefore not insulin deficient. Option C - Vitamin B12: Vitamin B12 can be a cause of neuropathy, leading to discomfort in legs. This is unlikely with normal levels of B12, methylmalonic acid, and homocysteine. Option D - Folate: Folate deficiency is unlikely to cause these symptoms, and the blood work indicates normal levels. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 37-year-old female presents with new onset fever, dyspnea and dry cough. She is currently on the ABVD regimen for Hodgkin’s lymphoma. Physical examination is significant for inspiratory crackles. Bleomycin-induced lung toxicity is suspected. Which of the following is a risk factor for bleomycin-induced lung toxicity?
questions.stemHtml: A 37-year-old female presents with new onset fever, dyspnea and dry cough. She is currently on the ABVD regimen for Hodgkin’s lymphoma. Physical examination is significant for inspiratory crackles. Bleomycin-induced lung toxicity is suspected. Which of the following is a risk factor for bleomycin-induced lung toxicity?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Renal insufficiency: Renal insufficiency is a risk factor for Bleomycin toxicity, as 80% of the drug is eliminated by the kidney. Logically this toxicity is dose dependent, with 6-18% of patients experiencing bleomycin-induced lung toxicity with doses of 360 units or more. Incorrect Options: Option A - High fraction of inspired oxygen: High fraction of inspired oxygen while on bleomycin and the contributions to subsequent toxicity are unclear, and have so far not been proven. Option B - Cigarette smoking: Similarly to inspired oxygen, the data on cigarette smoking is inconsistent regarding how much of an effect smoking has on bleomycin-induced lung toxicity. Option C - Simultaneous therapy with neupogen: In animal studies simultaneous therapy with neupogen was shown as a possible risk factor, however this has not been duplicated in human studies. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option D - Renal insufficiency:

  • Renal insufficiency is a risk factor for Bleomycin toxicity, as 80% of the drug is eliminated by the kidney. Logically this toxicity is dose dependent, with 6-18% of patients experiencing bleomycin-induced lung toxicity with doses of 360 units or more.

Option B - Cigarette smoking: Similarly to inspired oxygen, the data on cigarette smoking is inconsistent regarding how much of an effect smoking has on bleomycin-induced lung toxicity.

questions.stem: A 56 years old female was diagnosed with COPD 4 years. At her regular maintenance visit she asks about pneumococcal vaccine (PPSV23). She has never undergone a surgical procedure, she doesn’t take steroids, and she smokes 1 ppd. She doesn’t remember if she ever received PPSV23. The MOST appropriate recommendation is:
questions.stemHtml: A 56 years old female was diagnosed with COPD 4 years. At her regular maintenance visit she asks about pneumococcal vaccine (PPSV23). She has never undergone a surgical procedure, she doesn’t take steroids, and she smokes 1 ppd. She doesn’t remember if she ever received PPSV23. The MOST appropriate recommendation is:

options.label: B
options.text: Delay PPSV23 until the age of 65

options.label: C
options.text: Prescribe PPSV23 if she has frequent exacerbations

options.label: D
options.text: Prescribe PPSV23 if she begins inhaled steroids

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Administer PPSV23 single dose: There are two types of pneumococcal vaccines: A pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23; Pneumovax 23, Pnu-Immune) and a pneumococcal protein-conjugate vaccine (PCV13; Prevnar 13). Pneumococcal vaccination is recommended for all adults ≥65 years old and adults <65 years old who are at risk for pneumococcal infection or severe complications from pneumococcal infection. The decision regarding whether both PCV13 and PPSV23 are indicated and whether revaccination with PPSV23 is indicated vary based on patient age and risk factors. For adults ages 19 to 64 years with certain chronic conditions (chronic heart, lung, or liver disease, diabetes mellitus, smoking, alcohol use disorder), a single dose of PPSV23 is recommended (which applies to this patient, and is the correct answer). For adults with higher risk conditions (immunocompromised state, asplenia, cerebrospinal fluid leak, cochlear implant, or history of invasive pneumococcal disease), both PCV13 and PPSV23 should be given. PCV13 in addition to PPSV23 is not recommended unless the patient has an indication for PCV13 (immunocompromised state, and the other already noted indications) because the incidence of pneumococcal disease caused by PCV13 serotypes is very low. If both PCV13 and PPSV23 are indicated PCV13 should be given before PPSV23, and they should be given at separate time points to help ensure that protective antibodies to each vaccine develop. If the primary indication for vaccination is age ≥65 years, PPSV23 should be given ≥1 year after PCV13. Most experts recommend revaccination with PPSV23 for selected patients because immunity to polysaccharide vaccines wanes over time, but recommendations on revaccination vary among experts and clinical practice guidelines. Incorrect Options: Option B - Delay PPSV23 until the age of 65: The follow-up dose should be delayed until the age of 65 in patients who received the initial dose prior the age of 65. Some (but not all) experts recommend that at-risk individuals be revaccinated with PPSV23 at 5- to 10-year intervals because the antibody response to PPSV23 wanes over this time period. The optimal timing and number of vaccine doses needed to prevent disease are unknown and recommendations vary among experts and clinical practice guidelines. Option C - Prescribe PPSV23 if she has frequent exacerbations: Vaccination with PPSV23 should be administered based on age and primary diagnosis. An increase in the severity of symptoms is not an indication to accelerate vaccination. Option D - Prescribe PPSV23 if she begins inhaled steroids: Vaccination with PPSV23 should be done based on age and primary diagnosis. Escalation of treatment is not an indication to accelerate vaccination. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male who is a 30-pack/year smoker is currently being treated with first-line carboplatin and paclitaxel for metastatic squamous cell lung cancer. He has completed 4 cycles. CT scan is ordered for restaging. Unfortunately, imaging demonstrates progressive disease compared to the scan after 2 cycles. What treatment recommendations should be made?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male who is a 30-pack/year smoker is currently being treated with first-line carboplatin and paclitaxel for metastatic squamous cell lung cancer. He has completed 4 cycles. CT scan is ordered for restaging. Unfortunately, imaging demonstrates progressive disease compared to the scan after 2 cycles. What treatment recommendations should be made?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Nivolumab: Recent published data has demonstrated a clear benefit of nivolumab in the second-line setting for metastatic squamous cell carcinoma. Response rates and progression-free survival were also improved with nivolumab. This study has cemented nivolumab as the second-line agent for SCC of the lung. One should also check ROS1, ALK, and EGFR status to base treatment decisions. There is no need to continue chemotherapy when clear progression on treatment is demonstrated. Incorrect Options: Option A - Continue carbo-taxol for 2 more cycles: A head-to-head comparison of nivolumab to docetaxel demonstrated an overall survival benefit for nivolumab (9 vs. 6 months, respectively). Option B - Docetaxel: Docetaxel had worse outcomes compared to nivolumab in a randomized clinical trial. Option D - Single-agent pemetrexed: There is no need to continue chemotherapy when clear progression on treatment is demonstrated. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 68-year-old female presents with recurrent Graves' disease after having received one course of block and replacement therapy with carbimazole and thyroxine. After discussion, she elects to receive radioiodine treatment (RAI). Prior to receiving treatment she is rendered euthyroid again with carbimazole. At least how many days prior to her radioactive iodine should she stop her arbimazole?
questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old female presents with recurrent Graves' disease after having received one course of block and replacement therapy with carbimazole and thyroxine. After discussion, she elects to receive radioiodine treatment (RAI). Prior to receiving treatment she is rendered euthyroid again with carbimazole. At least how many days prior to her radioactive iodine should she stop her arbimazole?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - 7 days: In preparation for radioactive iodine (RAI) treatment in a patient with Graves' disease, discontinuing anti-thyroid medications like carbimazole is essential to ensure that the thyroid is no longer actively taking up iodine, which can interfere with the effectiveness of RAI. The recommended duration for discontinuing carbimazole before RAI is at least before 7 days. Incorrect Options: Option B - 14 days: Carbimazole needs to be stopped at least 7 days prior to radioiodine to ensure appropriate uptake Option C - 21 days: Carbimazole needs to be stopped at least 7 days prior to radioiodine to ensure appropriate uptake Option D - 28 days: Carbimazole needs to be stopped at least 7 days prior to radioiodine to ensure appropriate uptake @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a history of sarcoidosis, pulmonary fibrosis, and hyperlipidemia is admitted for community-acquired pneumonia. On the day after admission, she suddenly develops confusion and hypotension. The patient's blood pressure is 80/45 mmHg, and her heart rate is 105 bpm. Fingerstick testing indicates a glucose level of 40 mg/dL. She is immediately given 1 amp D50 and is started on IV fluids, but her blood pressure remains the same after a 2 L infusion. She is still hypotensive after norepinephrine is initiated. What is the next step in treatment?
questions.stemHtml:
A 45-year-old woman with a history of sarcoidosis, pulmonary fibrosis, and hyperlipidemia is admitted for community-acquired pneumonia. On the day after admission, she suddenly develops confusion and hypotension. The patient's blood pressure is 80/45 mmHg, and her heart rate is 105 bpm. Fingerstick testing indicates a glucose level of 40 mg/dL.
She is immediately given 1 amp D50 and is started on IV fluids, but her blood pressure remains the same after a 2 L infusion. She is still hypotensive after norepinephrine is initiated. What is the next step in treatment?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - IV hydrocortisone: This patient is in an adrenal crisis induced by the stress of her illness. Adrenal crisis is an exacerbation of adrenal insufficiency. It is life-threatening and due to decreased cortisol supply (e.g. discontinuing steroid therapy) or increased physiologic demand/stress (e.g. illness, surgery). It should be suspected in unexplained and refractory hypotension in a patient with predisposing factors. This patient has a history of sarcoidosis, which puts her at risk for an adrenal crisis for 2 reasons. Sarcoidosis is an infiltrative disorder that can affect the lungs and adrenal glands (leading to primary adrenal insufficiency) or pituitary-hypothalamus axis (leading to secondary adrenal insufficiency). In both cases, illness will increase physiologic demands for cortisol. Also, this patient's disease suggests that she has been treated with steroids for a prolonged period of time, and abrupt discontinuation of treatment can lead to a crisis. The first step in treating refractory hypotension is administering IV hydrocortisone because of its combined glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid effects. Administering a 100 mg bolus is standard before administering additional vasopressors. Alternatively, IV dexamethasone can be given. Incorrect Option s: Option A -IV normal saline: Cortisol deficiency leads to hypoglycemia. Patients in adrenal crisis should receive 5% dextrose in normal saline. Option B - Dobutamine: Failure to respond to fluid resuscitation and initiation of vasopressors suggest an adrenal crisis in this patient. Option D - IV methylprednisolone: Methylprednisolone is indicated to prevent an adrenal crisis on the day of scheduled surgery. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: You see a 35-year-old woman who was first diagnosed with prolactinoma three and a half years ago. At the time of diagnosis, she had galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, and suffered from headaches. An MRI pituitary test was taken at the time of diagnosis, which revealed a 13 mm pituitary adenoma. Since then, she has been treated with cabergoline and her current dose is 0.5 mg 1 tablet a week. The patient presented to the clinic after becoming pregnant. Her last MRI pituitary was taken 6 months prior to presentation and shows 8 mm pituitary adenoma. On physical examination, the patient appears well with a blood pressure of 110/78, a pulse of 88 beats per minute and a respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute. No abnormalities are noted. Laboratory test results 6 months ago revealed a prolactin level of 22 ug/L (normal:1-25 ug/L). What is the best next step in the management of this patient?
questions.stemHtml:
You see a 35-year-old woman who was first diagnosed with prolactinoma three and a half years ago. At the time of diagnosis, she had galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, and suffered from headaches. An MRI pituitary test was taken at the time of diagnosis, which revealed a 13 mm pituitary adenoma. Since then, she has been treated with cabergoline and her current dose is 0.5 mg 1 tablet a week.
The patient presented to the clinic after becoming pregnant. Her last MRI pituitary was taken 6 months prior to presentation and shows 8 mm pituitary adenoma.
On physical examination, the patient appears well with a blood pressure of 110/78, a pulse of 88 beats per minute and a respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute. No abnormalities are noted. Laboratory test results 6 months ago revealed a prolactin level of 22 ug/L (normal:1-25 ug/L).
What is the best next step in the management of this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Check serum prolactin measurements now and after 3 months of pregnancy

options.label: C
options.text: Conduct pituitary MRI without the use of gadolinium

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Discontinue cabergoline therapy now: In pregnant patients with prolactinomas, it is recommended that women discontinue dopamine agonist therapy as soon as they discover that they are pregnant. In selected patients, dopaminergic therapy may be continued in those who have macroadenomas and become pregnant, especially if patients have not had prior surgical or radiation therapy, and if the tumour is invasive or is abutting the optic chiasm. In our patient, her last pituitary MRI showed shrinkage of pituitary adenoma, and she does not have any evidence of an invasive tumour, hence, cabergoline therapy should be discontinued. Furthermore, microprolactinomas and macroprolactinomas that are localised to the sella were not found to undergo symptomatic growth during pregnancy. Incorrect Options: Option A - Check serum prolactin measurements now and after 3 months of pregnancy: Endocrine Society guidelines advise against performing serum prolactin measurements during pregnancy, as serum prolactin levels tend to increase 10-fold during pregnancy, and subsequent increases in prolactin levels do not accurately reflect changes in tumour growth or activity. Option B - Conduct formal visual field assessment: This patient did not report headaches or any visual field changes. Endocrine Society guidelines recommended formal visual field assessment in pregnant women with prolactinomas who experience severe headaches and/or visual field changes, but this patient does not have any visual field changes. Option C - Conduct pituitary MRI without the use of gadolinium: Endocrine Society guidelines advise against the use of routine pituitary MRI screening during pregnancy in patients with microadenomas or intrasellar macroadenomas unless there is clinical evidence for tumour growth, such as visual field compromise. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option D - Discontinue cabergoline therapy now:

  • In pregnant patients with prolactinomas, it is recommended that women discontinue dopamine agonist therapy as soon as they discover that they are pregnant. In selected patients, dopaminergic therapy may be continued in those who have macroadenomas and become pregnant, especially if patients have not had prior surgical or radiation therapy, and if the tumour is invasive or is abutting the optic chiasm. In our patient, her last pituitary MRI showed shrinkage of pituitary adenoma, and she does not have any evidence of an invasive tumour, hence, cabergoline therapy should be discontinued.
  • Furthermore, microprolactinomas and macroprolactinomas that are localised to the sella were not found to undergo symptomatic growth during pregnancy.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Check serum prolactin measurements now and after 3 months of pregnancy: Endocrine Society guidelines advise against performing serum prolactin measurements during pregnancy, as serum prolactin levels tend to increase 10-fold during pregnancy, and subsequent increases in prolactin levels do not accurately reflect changes in tumour growth or activity.

Option B - Conduct formal visual field assessment: This patient did not report headaches or any visual field changes. Endocrine Society guidelines recommended formal visual field assessment in pregnant women with prolactinomas who experience severe headaches and/or visual field changes, but this patient does not have any visual field changes.

Option C - Conduct pituitary MRI without the use of gadolinium: Endocrine Society guidelines advise against the use of routine pituitary MRI screening during pregnancy in patients with microadenomas or intrasellar macroadenomas unless there is clinical evidence for tumour growth, such as visual field compromise.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath and fatigue for the last 6 months. She reports her symptoms have been progressive and typically worsen with exertion, limiting her exercise tolerance such that she can only walk a block. Her vital signs are notable for an oxygen saturation of 89%. On physical examination, she has a loud pulmonic component of S2, prominent jugular venous pulsations, and a parasternal heave. She denies a history of chest discomfort or other medical problems. Which of the following is contributing to the pathogenesis of this patient’s lung disease?
questions.stemHtml:
A 45-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath and fatigue for the last 6 months. She reports her symptoms have been progressive and typically worsen with exertion, limiting her exercise tolerance such that she can only walk a block. Her vital signs are notable for an oxygen saturation of 89%. On physical examination, she has a loud pulmonic component of S2, prominent jugular venous pulsations, and a parasternal heave. She denies a history of chest discomfort or other medical problems.
Which of the following is contributing to the pathogenesis of this patient’s lung disease?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Decreased prostacyclin: Pulmonary hypertension is a condition characterized by increased pressures in the pulmonary vasculature. Patients typically present with subacute shortness of breath and fatigue such as in this case. Pulmonary hypertension is classified into 5 categories based on the underlying cause. Group 1 pulmonary hypertension, or pulmonary arterial hypertension, is the most likely underlying etiology in this case due to a lack of factors seen in other groups. This subtype is often idiopathic or genetic, but may occur in connective tissue diseases such as scleroderma, in HIV, and in schistosomiasis. The pathogenesis of this condition involves an imbalance in the levels of vasoactive molecules. Vasodilatory and anti-proliferation molecules such as nitric oxide and prostacyclin drop in these patients, leading to vasoconstriction, hypertrophy of all pulmonary vascular layers, and eventual fibrosis. Increased levels of vasoconstrictive molecules such as endothelin have a similar effect. Groups 2, 3, 4, and 5 describe pulmonary hypertension in the setting of left heart failure, intrinsic disease of the lung, chronic thromboembolic disease, and multifactorial etiologies, respectively. Incorrect Options: Option A - Decreased endothelin: Endothelin is a vasoconstrictor that increases in pulmonary hypertension. Option B - Increased nitric oxide: Nitric oxide is a vasodilator and anti-proliferative that decreases in pulmonary hypertension. Option D - Decreased left ventricular function: Decreased left ventricular function describes group 2 pulmonary hypertension. This patient has no evidence of or risk factors for congestive heart failure, making group 2 pathology less likely. @Neet_pg_bot

Groups 2, 3, 4, and 5 describe pulmonary hypertension in the setting of left heart failure, intrinsic disease of the lung, chronic thromboembolic disease, and multifactorial etiologies, respectively.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Decreased endothelin: Endothelin is a vasoconstrictor that increases in pulmonary hypertension.

She is receiving multiple medications and her GP is concerned about the risk of drug interactions particularly with respect to the risk of hypoglycaemia.
Which of the following drugs taken by this lady may result in an increased risk of hypoglycaemia in patients with diabetes?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Low dose aspirin: Low dose aspirin has been associated with the development of hypoglycaemia related to a stimulatory effect of aspirin on the beta cell-mediated via inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis. In larger doses, salicylates can have detrimental effects on glucose homeostasis resulting from inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation with a consequent impairment in glucose oxidation. Other commonly used agents which may increase the risk of hypoglycaemia, particularly in the elderly include ACE-inhibitors via mechanisms involving improved insulin sensitivity. Statins may have a diabetogenic risk. Nitrates and PPIs have no effect on glucose homeostasis, while nifedipine may have detrimental effects on glucose homeostasis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Isosorbide mononitrate: Nitrates and PPIs have no effect on glucose homeostasis Option B - Nifedipine: nifedipine may have detrimental effects on glucose homeostasis Option D - Omeprazole: Nitrates and PPIs have no effect on glucose homeostasis @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 63-year-old female is admitted with a history of COPD, in addition to multiple other medical problems. Due to worsening respiratory distress, she is transferred to the ICU. A review of previous pulmonary function tests will most likely reveal which of the following?
questions.stemHtml: A 63-year-old female is admitted with a history of COPD, in addition to multiple other medical problems. Due to worsening respiratory distress, she is transferred to the ICU. A review of previous pulmonary function tests will most likely reveal which of the following?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - FEV1 = 50-80% predicted and FEV1/FVC ≤70%: When reviewing pulmonary function tests, pay attention to certain details. Typically, a total lung capacity of >120% indicates hyperinflation, as seen in patients with chronic obstructive lung disease, while <80% would indicate restrictive lung disease. A ratio of FEV1/FVC is important in the determination of nature of abnormality, although it is age-dependent to a certain degree. In patients with COPD, it is <70%. A reduced ratio of FEV1/FVC may be seen in restrictive lung disease as well, but it is associated with a decreased total lung capacity. Combined restrictive and obstructive disease can alter the results of the tests. Incorrect Options: Option B - FEV1 = 80-85% predicted and FEV1/FVC ≥70%: A reduced ratio of FEV1/FVC may be seen in restrictive lung disease as well, but it is associated with a decreased total lung capacity. Option C - FEV1 = 110% predicted and FEV1/FVC ≤70%: A total lung capacity of >120% indicates hyperinflation, as seen in patients with chronic obstructive lung disease. Option D - FEV1 = 50-65% predicted and FEV1/FVC ≥50%: A reduced ratio of FEV1/FVC may be seen in restrictive lung disease as well, but it is associated with a decreased total lung capacity. @Neet_pg_bot

A reduced ratio of FEV1/FVC may be seen in restrictive lung disease as well, but it is associated with a decreased total lung capacity. Combined restrictive and obstructive disease can alter the results of the tests.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - FEV1 = 80-85% predicted and FEV1/FVC ≥70%: A reduced ratio of FEV1/FVC may be seen in restrictive lung disease as well, but it is associated with a decreased total lung capacity.

Option C - FEV1 = 110% predicted and FEV1/FVC ≤70%: A total lung capacity of >120% indicates hyperinflation, as seen in patients with chronic obstructive lung disease.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male with a 20-year history of type 1 diabetes is referred to the OPD after moving to the area for a new job. Amongst his notes you see that previous retinal screening classifies him as 'Retinopathy R1'. Which of these was therefore noted at his last retinal screening?
questions.stemHtml:
A 28-year-old male with a 20-year history of type 1 diabetes is referred to the OPD after moving to the area for a new job. Amongst his notes you see that previous retinal screening classifies him as 'Retinopathy R1'.
Which of these was therefore noted at his last retinal screening?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Microaneurysms: The National Screening Committee has produced guidance grading the lesions present on retinal screening. These are: R1 - background retinopathy - in this case microaneurysms R2 - pre-proliferative retinopathy R3 - proliferative retinopathy M - maculopathy P - photocoagulation U - ungradeable Incorrect Options: Option A - Detached macula: This is a more advanced stage of diabetic retinopathy and is not indicated by the classification 'R1'. Macular detachment can lead to significant vision loss and requires immediate medical attention. Option B - Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMAs): IRMAs are abnormal dilations and tortuosity of retinal blood vessels seen in more advanced stages of diabetic retinopathy. They are not typically classified as 'R1'. Option C - Venous beading: Venous beading is another characteristic feature of more advanced diabetic retinopathy, and it represents irregularities in the caliber of retinal veins. It is not indicated by the classification 'R1'. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option D - Microaneurysms:

The National Screening Committee has produced guidance grading the lesions present on retinal screening. These are:

  • R1 - background retinopathy - in this case microaneurysms
  • R2 - pre-proliferative retinopathy
  • R3 - proliferative retinopathy
  • M - maculopathy
  • P - photocoagulation
  • U - ungradeable

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Detached macula: This is a more advanced stage of diabetic retinopathy and is not indicated by the classification 'R1'. Macular detachment can lead to significant vision loss and requires immediate medical attention.

Option B - Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMAs): IRMAs are abnormal dilations and tortuosity of retinal blood vessels seen in more advanced stages of diabetic retinopathy. They are not typically classified as 'R1'.

Option C - Venous beading: Venous beading is another characteristic feature of more advanced diabetic retinopathy, and it represents irregularities in the caliber of retinal veins. It is not indicated by the classification 'R1'.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man reports to the OPD for high blood pressure readings found on several occasions, with systolic blood pressure persistently elevated above 160 mmHg. The patient also reports occasional symptoms of palpitation and shortness of breath. On physical examination, his heart rate is 112 beats per minute, blood pressure is 170/105 mmHg. Heart, lung and abdominal exams are non-revealing. No signs of clubbing or oedema present. Initial laboratory tests revealed sodium of 137 meq/L and potassium of 3 meq/L. The patient was admitted for hypokalaemia, and oral and intravenous potassium supplementation was started and his potassium level was corrected. Serum aldosterone and renin levels were 2441 pmol/L and 0.02 pmol/L (normal: 0.1-1.1 pmol/L), respectively, and cortisol level was 386 nmol/L. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast showed bilateral adrenal nodules, the right side nodule is 1.5 cm, and the left is a 0.6 cm nodule. Which of the following is the best next step for the diagnosis of this patient’s condition?

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Adrenal venous sampling: This patient clearly has hypertension diagnosed at a young age with hypokalaemia documented and corrected. He also has elevated aldosterone to renin ratio and suppressed plasma renin activity. aldosteronism is confirmed given his uncontrolled hypertension, suppressed renin activity, and high aldosterone. CT adrenal glands show bilateral nodules. Adrenal vein sampling (AVS) is a procedure entailing the measurement of aldosterone from both adrenal veins, to diagnose an adrenal source of excess aldosterone secretion. This should be the next step in the management of this patient. Incorrect Options: Option B - MRI adrenal gland: MRI has no advantage over CT in subtype evaluation of PA because it is more expensive and has less spatial resolution than CT. Option C - Right-sided adrenalectomy: Right-sided adrenalectomy is not the next option, because the adrenal source for aldosteronism is not confirmed yet, given the presence of bilateral adrenal nodules. Option D - Saline suppression test for aldosteronism: Serum aldosterone is not elevated, and plasma renin activity is not suppressed. Hence, there is no need for saline suppression tests to confirm high aldosterone secretion. @Neet_pg_bot

She is transferred from an outside community hospital with hypoxic respiratory failure. While in the ICU, she becomes acutely short of breath, is in tripod stance, and has severe hypoxemia on 100% bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) with a PaO2 of 62. Which finding would suggest flash pulmonary edema (FPE) as the cause of this patient's hypoxemia?

options.label: C

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Bilateral renal artery stenosis: Flash pulmonary edema (FPE) is a nonspecific clinical term used to describe a dramatic form of acute decompensated heart failure. Many common findings like heart failure, hypertension, coronary ischemia, valvular heart disease, and diastolic dysfunction are associated with acute decompensated heart failure as well as with FPE. Nevertheless, endothelial dysfunction (possibly secondary to excessive activity of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system) impaired nitric oxide synthesis, increased endothelin levels, and/or excessive circulating catecholamines may cause excessive pulmonary capillary permeability and facilitate FPE formation. Renal artery stenosis (chiefly bilateral) is a common cause of FPE. Lack of diurnal variation in blood pressure and widened pulse pressure are additional risk factors for FPE. Incorrect Options: Option B - Unilateral renal artery stenosis : Although unilateral renal artery stenosis can be a cause, it is less likely than bilateral. Option C - Normal left ventricular end diastolic pressure (LVEDP): Regardless of its etiology, an acute increase of LVEDP is essential for the development of FPE. Option D - Decreased LVEDP : An acute increase of LVEDP is essential for the development of FPE. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 63-year-old female with a history of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and chronic kidney disease stage 4 presents for the first time. She has been getting influenza vaccines yearly but was not aware of the availability of pneumococcal vaccines. Which vaccine(s) should she receive and why, according to the United States Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices?
questions.stemHtml: A 63-year-old female with a history of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and chronic kidney disease stage 4 presents for the first time. She has been getting influenza vaccines yearly but was not aware of the availability of pneumococcal vaccines. Which vaccine(s) should she receive and why, according to the United States Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices?

options.label: A
options.text: She should receive PCV13 (Prevnar 13) followed by PPSV23 (Pneumovax) 6-12 months later

options.label: D
options.text: She has no indication for pneumococcal vaccines

questions.solution: Correct Option B - She should only receive PPSV23: Infections due to Streptococcus pneumonia and invasive infections such as bacteremia and meningitis cause significant morbidity and mortality in children <2 years of age, adults 65 and older, and people with chronic conditions that interfere with fighting infections (e.g. malignancy, immunosuppression, asplenia). The highest mortality is observed among the elderly (65 and older). Vaccination is recommended for these vulnerable populations. The ACIP recommends pneumococcal vaccination for all adults ≥65 years old and adults <65 years old who are at risk for pneumococcal infection. Such risk factors include chronic heart disease (such as heart failure and cardiomyopathy, but excluding hypertension alone), chronic lung disease (such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic liver disease, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, current cigarette smoking, or alcohol use disorder). The decision to give both PCV13 and PPSV23 depend on patient age and risk status: Adults with higher risk conditions should receive both PCV13 and PPSV23. Such conditions are defined as being immunocompromised, having asplenia, or having structural abnormality that allows communication with the subarachnoid space such as a cerebrospinal fluid leak, or a cochlear implant. Also, those with a history of invasive pneumococcal disease are considered in the higher risk category and should receive both vaccines. When both PCV13 and PPSV23 are indicated, they should be given at separate time points to help ensure that protective antibodies to each vaccine develop. When possible, PCV13 should be given before PPSV23 For adults who have not received any pneumococcal vaccine previously, PCV13 should be given before PPSV23 (if PCV13 is indicated). If the primary indication for vaccination is age ≥65 years, PPSV23 should be given ≥1 year after PCV13. For adults between ages 19 and 64 years who require both vaccines, PPSV23 can be given ≥8 weeks after PCV13. In adults who have already received PPSV23, PCV13 should be given ≥1 year following PPSV23. Incorrect Options: Option A - She should receive PCV13 (Prevnar 13) followed by PPSV23 (Pneumovax) 6-12 months later: PCV13 is not recommended for healthy adults <65 years of age who are not immunocompromised, do not have asplenia, do not have a structural abnormality that allows communication with the subarachnoid space such as a cerebrospinal fluid leak, or a cochlear implant, or those without a history of invasive pneumococcal disease. Option C - She should only receive PCV13: If the primary indication for vaccination is age ≥65 years, PPSV23 should be given ≥1 year after PCV13. For adults between ages 19 and 64 years who require both vaccines, PPSV23 can be given ≥8 weeks after PCV13. Option D - She has no indication for pneumococcal vaccines: PPSV 23 (Pneumovax) alone is appropriate for this patient given her history of diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female patient returned after a ten days tour and presented with complaints of high fever and a fine petechial rash on the axilla, face, and extremities. The symptoms she experienced were similar to those she experienced two years earlier after return from the same mission. Those symptoms resolved with only symptomatic treatment. Today she was transported to the ER by her husband, who reports that the patient’s fever resolved two days ago, but this was followed by complaints of abdominal pain. This morning she appeared lethargic and ill. On exam, her skin is cool and blotchy, with circumoral cyanosis. Her pulse is weak and rapid and her blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg. She has a diffuse confluent petechial rash and her liver is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies are significant for platelet count of 70 cells/mL, white blood cell count of 2,000/mL, with predominant lymphocytosis, and increased serum aspartate aminotransferase. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these severe symptoms?

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Change in viral serotype: The patient’s condition is most likely due to a second infection with Dengue, but with a different viral serotype than the one that caused the same symptoms two years ago. Dengue fever is an acute febrile viral disease that typically results in headaches, joint pain, myalgia, rash, and leukopenia. It’s also known as “breakbone fever,” due to the characteristic severe joint pain. Dengue is widely distributed throughout tropical regions, transmitted by the Aedes mosquito. The causative organism is a single-stranded RNA virus - there are five serotypes (however, the fifth one is a sylvatic strain). The initial infection may be asymptomatic or only mildly symptomatic, but a second infection can be significantly more severe. This is thought to be the result of infection with a different serotype from the initial infection, leading to enhanced formation of immune complexes and acceleration of the T-lymphocyte response. The most severe manifestation of this viral infection can result in Dengue hemorrhagic fever, which is characterized by high fever and hemorrhagic signs, such as purpura, petechiae, and epistaxis; hepatomegaly, and circulatory failure/shock, which results from increased capillary permeability. Laboratory findings included thrombocytopenia. When evaluating a patient with acute fever, myalgia, lethargy, and a rash in addition to a history of travel to tropical/subtropical regions, both chikungunya and dengue fever should be in the differential diagnosis. The patient should be closely monitored if dengue is a possibility, since it can be life threatening. Circulatory collapse usually follows resolution of the initial fever by several days. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Blastocystis hominis: Blastocystis hominis, commonly referred to simply as blastocystis species, is the most common organism found while performing microscopic examinations of stool specimens in search of ova and parasites. Although these organisms are a frequent incidental finding in asymptomatic patients, in cases such as this when the patient is presenting with a diarrheal illness lasting more than a week, it is appropriate to initiate therapy with metronidazole. Incorrect Options: Option A - Giardia lamblia: Giardia lamblia is the most common protozoan organism implicated in symptomatic diarrheal illnesses, and it is responsible for approximately 5% of diarrheal illnesses in the United States and 15% of cases worldwide. It is not the most common organism found overall. Giardiasis is also standardly treated with metronidazole. Option B - Cryptosporidium parvum: Cryptosporidium parvum cases tend to aggregate more in the immunocompromised population, being responsible for approximately 16% of cases of diarrheal illness in patients with HIV. It usually resolves with the initiation of antiretroviral treatment. Option D - Entameba histolytica: Entamoeba histolytica is fairly uncommon in developed countries such as the United States. It is also standardly treated with metronidazole. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Place the patient on contact precautions until the patient is discharged from the hospital, regardless of improvement of symptoms: Preventing the spread of Clostridium difficile, the most common cause of hospital-acquired diarrhea and the most common nosocomial infection currently, involves placing the infected patients on contact precautions for the length of their hospital stay. questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl, who has been on follow-up with her neurosurgeon since 3 years of age for craniopharyngioma, is referred to the paediatric endocrinology clinic for short stature. She presented to the neurosurgeon with a headache and vomiting at 3 years of age. A CT scan of the brain was consistent with craniopharyngioma, causing obstructive hydrocephalus. A ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt was placed in situ following subtotal excision of the mass, which was then followed by radiotherapy. Multiple pituitary hormone deficiency (MPHD) was detected at the age of 6.5 years. She was started on hydrocortisone and levothyroxine at 7 years of age. Her height was 104 cm (5th centile); Ht SDS = -1.5 [predicted adult height 147.5 cm]. The patient’s body weight was 21.7 kg [>95th centile]. Bone age was consistent with chronological age. A follow-up MRI scan of the brain revealed a 2.5 x 3 cm2 residual mass in the pituitary-hypothalamic region. Serum IGF-1 level was 20 nmol/L (normal range 21.2-70.9 nmol/L). What would be the most appropriate treatment for this patient's short stature?

A 7-year-old girl, who has been on follow-up with her neurosurgeon since 3 years of age for craniopharyngioma, is referred to the paediatric endocrinology clinic for short stature. She presented to the neurosurgeon with a headache and vomiting at 3 years of age.

What would be the most appropriate treatment for this patient's short stature?

options.label: A
options.text: Arrange for further follow-up and wait for growth without growth hormone as it may increase the tumour’s size

options.label: B
options.text: Recombinant growth hormone in physiological doses

options.label: C
options.text: Recombinant growth hormone in supraphysiological doses

options.label: D
options.text: Recombinant growth hormone with a high dose of estradiol to achieve a greater final height

questions.answerText: Recombinant growth hormone in physiological doses
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Recombinant growth hormone in physiological doses: Growth hormone therapy in physiological doses is effective for achieving satisfactory height in short stature due to growth hormone deficiency in craniopharyngioma. Recombinant growth hormone in physiological doses is therefore recommended for this patient. Incorrect Options: Option A - Arrange for further follow-up and wait for growth without growth hormone as it may increase the tumour’s size: Growth hormone therapy has not been shown to adversely affect the growth of craniopharyngioma. Option C - Recombinant growth hormone in supraphysiological doses: A supraphysiological dose of growth hormone is not required (unlike in Turner syndrome) to achieve the expected height response in craniopharyngioma; recombinant growth hormone in supraphysiological doses is therefore incorrect. Option D - Recombinant growth hormone with a high dose of estradiol to achieve a greater final height: A high dose of estradiol might lead to premature epiphyseal fusion, blunting the height response to growth hormone and is, therefore, also incorrect. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option B - Recombinant growth hormone in physiological doses:

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Arrange for further follow-up and wait for growth without growth hormone as it may increase the tumour’s size: Growth hormone therapy has not been shown to adversely affect the growth of craniopharyngioma.

Option C - Recombinant growth hormone in supraphysiological doses: A supraphysiological dose of growth hormone is not required (unlike in Turner syndrome) to achieve the expected height response in craniopharyngioma; recombinant growth hormone in supraphysiological doses is therefore incorrect.

Option D - Recombinant growth hormone with a high dose of estradiol to achieve a greater final height:  A high dose of estradiol might lead to premature epiphyseal fusion, blunting the height response to growth hormone and is, therefore, also incorrect.

questions.stem: Treatment an HIV patient co-infected with hepatitis B would include which of the following combinations of antiretroviral drugs which have been shown to be highly efficacious in co-infected patients.
questions.stemHtml: Treatment an HIV patient co-infected with hepatitis B would include which of the following combinations of antiretroviral drugs which have been shown to be highly efficacious in co-infected patients.
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Tenofovir + emtricitabine: Co-infection with HIV and hepatitis B is a fairly common scenario, with 10% of HIV patients also harboring an active infection with hepatitis B. Due to the similar risk factors for the acquisition of HIV and hepatitis B such as sexual contact and IV drug use, data have shown that up to 90% of HIV patients have serological evidence of a resolved hepatitis B infection. Tenofovir and emtricitabine, both nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTI), comprise the recommended combination of antiretrovirals for patients with hepatitis B and HIV co-infection. The most active drug in the combination is emtricitabine. Emtricitabine given alone does have significant activity toward both HIV and hepatitis B, with a lack of major adverse effects. Incorrect Options: Option B - Lamivudine + emtricitabine: It is not recommended to administer lamivudine with emtricitabine in general due to a competitive effect produced from both drugs due to a similar mechanism of action. Option C - Abacavir + tenofovir + lamivudine: The combination of abacavir, tenofovir, and lamivudine is not recommended for HIV and hepatitis B co-infection. Furthermore, this combination should be avoided if possible for the treatment of HIV patients in general due to the tendency for each of these drugs to select for drug-resistant mutations and produce virologic failure in up to 50% of patients. Option D - Zidovudine + lamivudine + efavirenz: The side effect profile of the combination of zidovudine, efavirenz, and lamivudine outweighs any potential benefit obtained from combining these drugs. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Cryoglobulins: Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis is caused by the vascular deposition of circulating immune complexes predominantly in small blood vessels. There are 3 main categories of cryoglobulinemia: Type I cryoglobulinemia, which is often asymptomatic and associated with lymphoproliferative disorders, consists of a single monoclonal immunoglobulin. Type II and III (or mixed) cryoglobulins are immune complexes, that contain either monoclonal (type II) or polyclonal (type III) IgMs with rheumatoid factor activity and are most often responsible for the clinical presentation of cryoglobulinemia. The main features of the disease are generalised arthralgia, orthostatic skin purpura and low C4 in the presence of circulating cryoglobulins. There may be renal involvement in the form of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and peripheral neuropathy. The neuropathy can present as a mild sensory neuropathy, but also as a motor neuropathy, which is often sudden in onset and presents as an asymmetric mononeuritis. Many patients have sicca symptoms although do not meet the full criteria for Sjörgren's syndrome and the ENA screen is usually negative. Incorrect Options: Option A - ANCA (Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies): ANCA is typically associated with small vessel vasculitis, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) or microscopic polyangiitis (MPA). questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with a non-healing wound. He previously suffered a traumatic crush injury to his anterior thigh requiring debridement and attempted skin graft reconstruction, which subsequently failed. He has been lost to follow-up for almost a year and now presents with a persistent ulcer measuring 3 cm x 3 cm. What is the next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man presents with a non-healing wound. He previously suffered a traumatic crush injury to his anterior thigh requiring debridement and attempted skin graft reconstruction, which subsequently failed. He has been lost to follow-up for almost a year and now presents with a persistent ulcer measuring 3 cm x 3 cm. What is the next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue wet to dry dressing changes

options.label: B
options.text: Place a negative pressure dressing and re-examine in 2 weeks

options.label: D
options.text: Assess nutritional status and encourage abstaining from tobacco

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Biopsy the ulcer: This patient has a persistent, non-healing wound for almost a year. The continuous cycle of partial healing followed by inflammation over a long period of time can predispose him to malignant degeneration. Before attempting any changes in wound management or reconstruction, malignancy should be thoroughly ruled out by biopsy. questions.stem: A 30-year-old male has a persistent “lump” in his anterior thigh after sustaining a minor trauma 4 weeks ago. On exam, he has a fixed mass that is approximately 4 x 4 cm in the soft tissues of his anterior thigh. His overlying abrasions are healing well. What is the next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old male has a persistent “lump” in his anterior thigh after sustaining a minor trauma 4 weeks ago. On exam, he has a fixed mass that is approximately 4 x 4 cm in the soft tissues of his anterior thigh. His overlying abrasions are healing well. What is the next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat exam in 10 weeks to confirm resolution of his hematoma

options.label: B
options.text: Obtain CT scan of the chest, order LDH level, and schedule an incisional biopsy in the operating room

options.label: C
options.text: Obtain a core-needle biopsy in the office and a radiograph of the extremity

options.label: D
options.text: Proceed with a wide local excision with 3 cm margins and rotational flap reconstruction

questions.answerText: Obtain a core-needle biopsy in the office and a radiograph of the extremity
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Obtain a core-needle biopsy in the office and a radiograph of the extremity This situation should raise suspicion for a soft tissue sarcoma. Not uncommonly, a minor trauma may bring attention to an underlying mass that is otherwise asymptomatic. This patient’s workup should be approached systematically. After a complete history and physical exam, a plain radiograph and office biopsy should be the first step. Without a definitive diagnosis, aggressive surgical planning is not appropriate at this time. If the biopsy reveals a neoplastic process, further imaging should be obtained, with MRI being the test of choice for extremity sarcoma (CT scan is used for retroperitoneal sarcomas). Chest imaging should be obtained to assess for metastatic disease (radiograph vs CT scan depending on overall suspicion). Other options for biopsy include FNA, image-guided core needle or FNA, or incisional biopsy. Occasionally with small lesions, an excisional biopsy can be used. With any type of biopsy, the placement of incisions and biopsies should be thoughtful since they will need to be fully resected during definitive wide local excision. Ideally, the same surgeon who will be performing the definitive resection should perform the biopsy. Incorrect Options: Option A - Repeat exam in 10 weeks to confirm resolution of his hematoma: A short interval exam (1-2 weeks) is reasonable, but a 10-week interval without a definitive diagnosis is not recommended. Option B - Obtain CT scan of the chest, order LDH level, and schedule an incisional biopsy in the operating room: Diagnosis of the primary lesion should be obtained if possible before any additional staging or operative planning. Performing an incisional biopsy in the operating room may add unneeded expense and morbidity for this patient and may compromise future surgical planning if done incorrectly. Option D - Proceed with a wide local excision with 3 cm margins and rotational flap reconstruction: This may eventually be required, but the diagnosis should be established first followed by appropriate staging. High-grade or large lesions may benefit from neoadjuvant therapy before surgery. @Neet_pg_bot

KOH examination of the hairs reveals infected hair filled with hyphae producing bubbles of gas. What is the most likely cause of this condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Trichophyton schoenleinii: Scutula formation, chronicity, and extensive hair loss are clinically consistent with tinea favosa (favus), a severe form of tinea capitis caused by T. schoenleinii. In tinea favosa, upon exposure to KOH, there is bubbling of KOH through the air spaces between hyphae elements. Incorrect Options: Option A - Trichophyton rubrum: T.rubrum is not detected by yellow-crusted plaques and extensive hair loss or a peripheral scutula formation as well. Option B - Trichophyton tonsurans: This severe form of hair infection is not typical of other causes of tinea capitis such as T. tonsurans Option C - Microsporum canis: M. canis also is known to cause severe hair loss. Rarely, favus is caused by Trichophyton violaceum, Trichophyton mentagrophytes var quinckeanum, or Microsporum gypseum. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Urodynamics: The patient’s voiding dysfunction may be related to BPH and outlet obstruction, diabetic cystopathy with poor sensation and detrusor function, or both. questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with a rapid onset of a fever, nausea, vomiting, and pain in the lower abdomen and groin. She started feeling unwell overnight and noticed a painful, macular rash extending from her groin and lower abdomen. She recently went for her usual hair-removal appointment but this time complained of scattered pustular folliculitis that started 3 days ago. The patient denies vaginal discharge, frequency, urgency, or dysuria. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. She has no significant past medical history. The patient appears acutely unwell and restless due to a painful lower abdomen. Her vital signs are as follows: temperature 104.1°F, regular pulse rate 110 bpm, and blood pressure 104/68. Laboratory investigations confirm multi-organ failure with coagulopathy. Blood cultures, skin swabs, and throat swabs are sent for Gram stain, culture, and sensitivities. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and hematuria. A chest radiograph shows widespread bilateral infiltrates. What is the most likely primary diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml:
A 35-year-old woman presents with a rapid onset of a fever, nausea, vomiting, and pain in the lower abdomen and groin. She started feeling unwell overnight and noticed a painful, macular rash extending from her groin and lower abdomen. She recently went for her usual hair-removal appointment but this time complained of scattered pustular folliculitis that started 3 days ago. The patient denies vaginal discharge, frequency, urgency, or dysuria. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. She has no significant past medical history.
The patient appears acutely unwell and restless due to a painful lower abdomen. Her vital signs are as follows: temperature 104.1°F, regular pulse rate 110 bpm, and blood pressure 104/68. Laboratory investigations confirm multi-organ failure with coagulopathy. Blood cultures, skin swabs, and throat swabs are sent for Gram stain, culture, and sensitivities. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and hematuria. A chest radiograph shows widespread bilateral infiltrates. What is the most likely primary diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome: Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome typically emerges from group A Streptococcus (GAS) infection such as Streptococcus pyogenes in areas of minor injury or surgery. The onset of symptoms is rapid and frequently consists of pain that precedes tenderness or is out of proportion with the physical examination. Other common symptoms include fever, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Confusion and coma have also been documented. The majority of patients have signs of soft tissue infection characterized by swelling and erythema. Progression to necrotizing fasciitis or myositis occurs in as many as 70% of patients. Clinicians should note necrotizing fasciitis may involve GAS, C. perfringens, or C. septicum. Of additional concern is the development of vesicles that become bullae and later violaceous, indicative of spreading necrotizing infection. Without prompt treatment, the condition advances rapidly. It requires urgent surgical exploration, debridement, fasciotomy, or amputation. Septicemic shock and multiorgan failure develop within hours. Immediate treatment of septic shock reduces mortality, and management should proceed as per normal protocols with particular attention to aggressive IV hydration. Differentiating between staphylococcal or streptococcal toxic shock syndromes on clinical grounds is difficult. Therefore, administering clindamycin with penicillin is preferred until bacterial isolates are obtained. Other options include vancomycin or a first-generation cephalosporin. Incorrect Options: Option A - Acute respiratory distress syndrome: Renal impairment, coagulopathy, deranged liver function tests, and acute respiratory distress syndrome are the most common complications. Option B - Clostridium perfringens infection: Crepitations may be palpated beneath the surface of erythema and be an indication of gas gangrene caused by C. perfringens. Option D - Meningococcal septicemia: Meningococcal septicemia may be considered with symptoms consistent with septicemia. However, the description of the rash is not consistent. The rash of meningococcal septicemia is a characteristic non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash. Patients often have a prodrome of upper respiratory symptoms such as a sore throat or a cough as well as a headache. @Neet_pg_bot

She complains of pain in her left knee with an effusion detectable. Investigations: Hand X-rays: "soft tissue swelling to the right middle finger with periostial elevation seen at the middle phalanx of that finger". Synovial fluid aspirate Left Knee: Clear straw coloured synovial fluid, no organisms seen, and white cells at 500 µ/L (90% Lymphocytes, 10% neutrophils). The patient is needle phobic and refuses blood testing. Which is the likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml:
A 4-year-old girl is brought by her parents with a 2-week history of pain and swelling in her hands and feet. There is a dactylitis to the right middle finger and left second toe. She complains of pain in her left knee with an effusion detectable.
Investigations:
Hand X-rays: "soft tissue swelling to the right middle finger with periostial elevation seen at the middle phalanx of that finger".
Synovial fluid aspirate Left Knee: Clear straw coloured synovial fluid, no organisms seen, and white cells at 500 µ/L (90% Lymphocytes, 10% neutrophils).
The patient is needle phobic and refuses blood testing.
Which is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Sickle cell anaemia: Sickle cell disease is more common in Africa, and parts of Greece, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. It has an autosomal recessive inheritance. Arthritis can occur in a migratory pattern as well as causing dactylitis. Painful crises are typical features of the condition. Other complications include osteonecrosis of the femoral head, osteomyelitis of long tubular bones, & septic arthritis. Painful veno-occlusive crises can occur. Precipitants of crises include cold, emotional stress, pregnancy, & travelling at high altitudes. MRI may be more sensitive than X-ray in detecting osteonecrosis. X-ray features can include periostitis / periosteal elevation but these resolve after several months. Incorrect answers - Incorrect Options: Option A - Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA): The above diagnosis is not suggestive of Juvenile idiopathic arthritis. The above diagnosis is suggestive of Sickle cell anaemia. Option B - Sarcoidosis is incorrect: Viral infection and sarcoidosis are not entirely compatible diagnoses. Lymphocytes are predominantly found in the synovial fluid. Option C - Septic arthritis: Viral infection and sarcoidosis are not entirely compatible diagnoses. In septic arthritis, high pus cell count and thick/turbid aspirate are seen. @Neet_pg_bot

A chest radiograph shows a cavitary infiltrate with an air-fluid level in the right upper lobe (RUL). What is the presumptive diagnosis, and what is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.stemHtml:
A 50-year-old man with a history of hypertension, seizures, and alcohol abuse presents to the ER after a few weeks of a productive cough, difficulty breathing, a fever, and chills.
On the physical exam, his temperature is 102.5 degrees Fahrenheit, and his HR is 110 bpm. Diminished breath sounds are noted in the right upper lobe (RUL). A chest radiograph shows a cavitary infiltrate with an air-fluid level in the right upper lobe (RUL).
What is the presumptive diagnosis, and what is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: Non-small cell lung cancer and surgical resection

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Lung abscess and ampicillin-sulbactam: Most lung abscesses result from aspiration of oral secretions. Patients who are predisposed usually have a history of altered sensorium such as chronic alcohol use disorder, seizure, coma, anesthesia, drug overdose, or stroke. Lung abscesses are caused by mixed aerobic and anaerobic bacteria from the oral flora. They are diagnosed on chest radiographs as a cavitary infiltrate with an air-fluid level that may be surrounded by a thick wall. This clinical presentation is usually insidious over weeks to months and is associated with a productive cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, fevers, tachycardia, chills, and night sweats. Lung abscesses are commonly found in the upper lung fields and the right lower lobe. Useful mnemonics to help remember obligate aerobes vs anaerobes: Obligate aerobes: “If No AER, Anthrax and TB can’t survive!” No = NOcardia Aer = pseudomonas AERuginosa Anthrax = B. anthracis TB = M. tuberculosis Microaerophils = “bacters”: Campylobacter, Helicobacter Obligate anaerobes: "These BACTERia ACTIN CLOSTRophobic environments (non-healing ulcers): BACTERia = Bacteroides (E.G., B. fragilis) ACTIN = Actinomyces CLOSTRophobic = CLOSTRidium Treatment includes intravenous antibiotics in addition to postural drainage. Empiric regimens should be agents that penetrate the lung parenchyma and treat both strict anaerobes and facultatively anaerobic streptococci such as ampicillin-sulbactam or a carbapenem. Formerly, clindamycin was the preferred agent, but most experts now avoid it as a first choice due to the associated risk of Clostridioides (formerly Clostridium difficile) infection. Incorrect Options: Option A - Non-small cell lung cancer and surgical resection: Non-small cell lung cancer cannot be diagnosed on a chest x-ray; a needle biopsy must be performed. Treatment for stage 1 includes surgical resection, which is associated with a 5-year survival rate in 70% of cases. Option B - Aspiration pneumonia and clindamycin: Aspiration pneumonia typically presents with focal or patchy consolidation and is commonly found in the right lower lobe. Clindamycin can be used for treatment. Option D - Pulmonary embolism and heparin: Pulmonary embolism is diagnosed with helical CT, and treatment includes unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option C - Lung abscess and ampicillin-sulbactam:

  • Most lung abscesses result from aspiration of oral secretions. Patients who are predisposed usually have a history of altered sensorium such as chronic alcohol use disorder, seizure, coma, anesthesia, drug overdose, or stroke. Lung abscesses are caused by mixed aerobic and anaerobic bacteria from the oral flora. They are diagnosed on chest radiographs as a cavitary infiltrate with an air-fluid level that may be surrounded by a thick wall. This clinical presentation is usually insidious over weeks to months and is associated with a productive cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, fevers, tachycardia, chills, and night sweats. Lung abscesses are commonly found in the upper lung fields and the right lower lobe.
  • Useful mnemonics to help remember obligate aerobes vs anaerobes:

Obligate aerobes:

  • “If No AER, Anthrax and TB can’t survive!”
    • No = NOcardia
    • Aer = pseudomonas AERuginosa
    • Anthrax = B. anthracis
    • TB = M. tuberculosis
  • Microaerophils = “bacters”:  Campylobacter, Helicobacter
  • Obligate anaerobes:  "These BACTERia ACTIN CLOSTRophobic environments (non-healing ulcers):
    • BACTERia = Bacteroides (E.G., B. fragilis)
    • ACTIN = Actinomyces
    • CLOSTRophobic = CLOSTRidium
  • Treatment includes intravenous antibiotics in addition to postural drainage. Empiric regimens should be agents that penetrate the lung parenchyma and treat both strict anaerobes and facultatively anaerobic streptococci such as ampicillin-sulbactam or a carbapenem. Formerly, clindamycin was the preferred agent, but most experts now avoid it as a first choice due to the associated risk of Clostridioides (formerly Clostridium difficile) infection. 

Incorrect Options: 

Option A - Non-small cell lung cancer and surgical resection: Non-small cell lung cancer cannot be diagnosed on a chest x-ray; a needle biopsy must be performed. Treatment for stage 1 includes surgical resection, which is associated with a 5-year survival rate in 70% of cases.

Option B - Aspiration pneumonia and clindamycin: Aspiration pneumonia typically presents with focal or patchy consolidation and is commonly found in the right lower lobe. Clindamycin can be used for treatment.

Option D - Pulmonary embolism and heparin: Pulmonary embolism is diagnosed with helical CT, and treatment includes unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin.

questions.stemHtml:

Vital signs are as follows: blood pressure 149/92 mm Hg, heart rate 95 beats/min, respirations 22 breaths/min, temperature 37.9° Celsius (100.2° Fahrenheit), and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. On chest examination, dullness to percussion and coarse inspiratory crackles are noted at the left lung base. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. A chest radiograph shows opacification of the left lower lobe with air bronchograms and no evidence of effusion or interstitial edema.
Which of the following is the initial empiric antibiotic for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid plus azithromycin This patient has community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), which is primarily caused by Streptococcus. Because she is rather young, has stable vital signs, and not excessively hypoxic, she should be treated as an outpatient. The most appropriate agent will cover gram-positive organisms, gram-negative rods, and atypical causes of pneumonia. Current recommendations for treating outpatient pneumonia in patients with major comorbidities (such as COPD in this patient) or recent antibiotic use broadly include one of two options. Dual therapy options include using a beta-lactam (amoxicillin or amoxicillin/clavulanic acid) plus either a macrolide (erythromycin, roxithromycin, azithromycin or clarithromycin) or doxycycline. The other option is monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone. However, monotherapy treatment with a fluoroquinolone is discouraged in ambulatory patients with CAP without comorbid conditions or recent antimicrobial use unless there is a high local prevalence of both macrolide-resistant and doxycycline-resistant S. pneumoniae and an alternative regimen is not feasible. Incorrect Options: Option A - Azithromycin: Azithromycin would not be indicated as monotherapy for CAP in areas like the United States with high (>25%) macrolide resistance. They are part of the 2009 British Thoracic Society guidelines, as the United Kingdom has lower macrolide resistance. Option B - Clarithromycin: Carithromycin would not be indicated as monotherapy for CAP in areas like the United States with high (>25%) macrolide resistance Option D - Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole is a combination antibiotic that would have insufficient coverage against organisms responsible for community-acquired pneumonia. The most common use of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole is in the setting of urinary tract infections, ear infections, some upper respiratory infections, and some gastrointestinal illnesses. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 68-year-old female bone marrow biopsy confirmed AML is sent for chemotherapy. The patient's consultant contacts you, concerned, and asks whether or not it is safe to place a PICC or port with her current platelet count. What is the platelet count threshold to trigger prophylactic platelet transfusion prior to placement of a central venous catheter?
questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old female bone marrow biopsy confirmed AML is sent for chemotherapy. The patient's consultant contacts you, concerned, and asks whether or not it is safe to place a PICC or port with her current platelet count. What is the platelet count threshold to trigger prophylactic platelet transfusion prior to placement of a central venous catheter?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - ≤ 20,000/μL: The AABB (formerly the American Association of Blood Banks) developed guidelines for the appropriate use of platelet transfusion (Kauffman et al., Ann Intern Med 2015). These published recommendations were based on randomized clinical trials and observational studies (published between 1900 and September 2014) reporting clinical outcomes on patients receiving prophylactic or therapeutic platelet transfusions. The guidelines make the following 6 recommendations: Hospitalized patients with therapy-induced hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia should be transfused prophylactically to reduce the risk for spontaneous bleeding for a platelet count of ≤ 10,000/μL. In these patients, The AABB recommends transfusing up to a single apheresis unit or equivalent. Patients undergoing elective central venous catheter placement should receive prophylactic platelet transfusion for a platelet count less ≤ 20,000/μL. Patients having elective diagnostic lumbar puncture should receive prophylactic platelet transfusion for a platelet count less ≤ 50,000/μL. Patients undergoing major elective nonneuraxial surgery should receive prophylactic platelet transfusion for a platelet count less ≤ 50,000/μL. Patients who are nonthrombocytopenic and undergo cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass should NOT receive routine prophylactic platelet transfusion. However, those patients undergoing bypass surgery who experience perioperative bleeding with thrombocytopenia and/or evidence of platelet dysfunction should receive prophylactic platelet transfusion. The AABB cannot recommend for or against platelet transfusion for patients receiving antiplatelet therapy who have intracranial hemorrhage (traumatic or spontaneous). The rest of the options are wrong. @Neet_pg_bot
