questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements best reflects our current understanding of the physiology of the pleural space?

options.label: A
options.text: Absorption of pleural fluid is effectuated by uptake by capillaries

options.label: B
options.text: Liquid, proteins, and other molecules are actively transported through mesothelial cells into the pleural space

options.label: C
options.text: Pressure gradient between the pleural space and interstitial space in which the intrapleural pressure > interstitial pressure

options.label: D
options.text: Molecules, proteins, and liquid move passively

questions.answerText: Molecules, proteins, and liquid move passively
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Molecules, proteins, and liquid move passively: The pleural space consists of two cellular layers, a superficially located mesothelial layer and an underlying connective tissue layer. These membrane have been shown to be leaky, enabling the occurrence of passive movement of molecules, proteins, and liquid. Incorrect Options: Option A - Absorption of pleural fluid is effectuated by uptake by capillaries: The uptake by capillaries in the absorption of pleural fluid does not coincide with our current understanding of pleural fluid physiology. Option B - Liquid, proteins, and other molecules are actively transported through mesothelial cells into the pleural space: Similarly, the active transport of liquid, proteins, and other molecules to the pleural space through mesothelial cells was been shown to be false, this is due to the fact that mesothelial cells do not generate an electrical potential which would be present in cells which are performing active transport. Option C - Pressure gradient between the pleural space and interstitial space in which the intrapleural pressure > interstitial pressure: In order to allow passive transport of fluid, the interstitial pressure should be greater than the pleural pressure. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option D - Molecules, proteins, and liquid move passively:

  • The pleural space consists of two cellular layers, a superficially located mesothelial layer and an underlying connective tissue layer. These membrane have been shown to be leaky, enabling the occurrence of passive movement of molecules, proteins, and liquid.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Absorption of pleural fluid is effectuated by uptake by capillaries: The uptake by capillaries in the absorption of pleural fluid does not coincide with our current understanding of pleural fluid physiology.

Option B - Liquid, proteins, and other molecules are actively transported through mesothelial cells into the pleural space: Similarly, the active transport of liquid, proteins, and other molecules to the pleural space through mesothelial cells was been shown to be false, this is due to the fact that mesothelial cells do not generate an electrical potential which would be present in cells which are performing active transport.

Option C - Pressure gradient between the pleural space and interstitial space in which the intrapleural pressure > interstitial pressure:  In order to allow passive transport of fluid, the interstitial pressure should be greater than the pleural pressure.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male with refractory B-cell acute lymphoid leukemia (B-ALL, dx 6 months ago) is admitted to ICU with acute neutropenic septic shock secondary to klebsiella bacteremia. He is currently on ECOG 1910 regimen and takes Lovenox for atrial fibrillation. He has a history of pulmonary embolism. There no other associated symptoms like chest pain, cough, nausea, vomiting, rash, or headaches. However, he reports 1-2 days of diarrhea. The patient is intubated due to inability to compensate for severe metabolic acidosis due to suspected likely gut translocation. Echocardiogram shows mildly dilated LA. LVEF is 60%. He has no valvular abnormalities and normal ventricular contractility. Chest X-ray shows increasing airspace opacities, bilateral lung bases, and midzone alveolar edema. Pneumonia is excluded. The patient has a persistent, small left pleural effusion with associated slight basal atelectasis. Arterial blood gas shows an oxygen tension of 198 mmHg with a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.8. What information is lacking that precludes a diagnosis of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)?

options.label: A
options.text: There is no indication of CPAP or PEEP.

options.label: B
options.text: Berlin definition includes only new respiratory failure and not worsening respiratory symptoms.

options.label: C
options.text: Any pleural effusion would prevent attaching any importance to lung opacities

options.text: Cardiac failure cannot be excluded without information of pulmonary arterial wedge pressure.

questions.answerText: There is no indication of CPAP or PEEP.
questions.solution: Correct Option A -There is no indication of CPAP or PEEP. This information does not provide any information of PEEP. The following are the components of the Berlin criteria for ERDS diagnosis that have superseded the American-European Consensus Conference (AECC definition): Presence of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure criteria Onset within 1 week of insult, or new (within 7 days) or worsening respiratory symptoms Bilateral airspace disease on chest X-ray or computed tomography not fully explained by effusions, lobar or lung collapse, or nodules Cardiac failure not the primary cause of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure This definition has many limitations. For instance, the term "acute onset" is not defined (i.e. within hours, days, or weeks); the degree of hypoxemia may vary significantly depending on PEEP levels; the agreement in interpretation of radiological findings remains modest, even between experts. Threshold values of PCWP <18 mmHg (in the case of measurement) are not always discriminative, since many patients with ARDS exhibit values >18 mmHg, due to increased intrathoracic pressure or fluid overload after resuscitation. Finally, the term ALI is commonly misused, referring to both patients with 200 < FiO2 < 300 mmHg and those suffering from ARDS with FiO2 < 200. questions.solution: Correct Option B- 1: The CURB-65 is a criteria used to identify patients who can be managed as outpatients or inpatients. It is also used as a severity score to predict mortality due to community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). It consists of 5 variables; each scored 1 point. These include: New-onset confusion Urea > 7mmol/L Respiratory rate > 30/min Systolic blood pressure (SBP)< 90mmHg or diastolic blood pressure (DBP)< 60mmHg Age > 65 years As this patient had no confusion, urea <7mmol/L, SBP<90mmHg, DBP<60mmHg, is below 65 years of age, and respiratory rate of 31, the CURB-65 totals up to 1. Patients with a score of 0-1 can be treated as outpatients. Patients with a score of 2 require hospital-supervised treatment. It can be a short-stay inpatient or hospital-supervised outpatient treatment. Patients with a score of 3 or more should be managed for severe pneumonia in the hospital. Patients with a score of 4 and 5 require intensive care treatment. Option C- 2: The patient meets no variable other than the respiratory rate to fulfil the CURB-65 criteria; hence the score cannot exceed 1. Option D- 3: The patient meets no variable other than the respiratory rate to fulfil the CURB-65 criteria; hence the score cannot exceed 1. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman presents with complaints of low-grade fever, chest pain, and productive cough for the last 6 weeks. She has also lost 6 kg of weight over 3 months. On examination, there are enlarged and matted cervical lymph nodes. Chest examination is unremarkable. The interferon-gamma release assay came out positive. The chest X-ray shows bilateral mediastinal lymphadenopathy. A transbronchial needle biopsy is taken that shows caseating granuloma. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Nivolumab: Randomized, phase III data demonstrates an improvement in survival and less toxicity for nivolumab compared to chemotherapy as second-line systemic therapy for patients with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This is true of both squamous and nonsquamous histologies. Thus, the NCCN Guidelines lists immune checkpoint inhibitors as the preferred choice in this clinical setting. Borghaei et al. (N Eng J Med, 2015) performed a randomized, phase III trial in 582 patients with stage IV nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who had progressed during or after platinum-based doublet chemotherapy. Patients were randomized to nivolumab (3 mg/kg every 2 weeks) or docetaxel (75 mg/m2 every 3 weeks). The primary end point was overall survival. Nivolumab resulted in improved median overall survival (12.2 vs. 9.4 months, p=0.002), 18-month overall survival (39% vs. 23%), and objective response (19% vs. 12%, p=0.02). Nivolumab resulted in superior outcomes in all groups when divided by programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) proportion score. Furthermore, the nivolumab arm had a lower incidence of grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events (10% vs. 54%). Rest of the options are irrelevant in this case. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Review of medications If the associated rate of SMVT is rapid enough to result in hemodynamic compromise, presyncope, or syncope with deterioration into cardiac arrest may occur. The patient's medication list should be reviewed carefully, with special attention to rate-controlling drugs and antiarrhythmic drugs, to assess potential proarrhythmic effects and to guide therapy. This patient presented initially in AF with aberrant conduction to the ventricle. The degree of aberration is variable. AF is confirmed by the irregularity of the rhythm as well as the narrow complex beats on the right side of the tracing with identical morphology to the prior ECG in sinus rhythm. The wide complex rhythm during AF additionally does not meet Brugada or Vereckei criteria for VT. The final ECG demonstrates sustained monomorphic VT as demonstrated by fusion complexes, low high activation, a QS complex lead V6, a slurred downstroke in lead V1 (Josephson sign), R wave-to-peak time >50 ms in lead II, and a notch in the downslope of aVR. The other options are irrelevant in this scenario. The Brugada Criteria are summarized below. The more recent and simpler Vereckei criteria are also below. If the presenting ECG was interpreted as polymorphic VT, cardiac catheterization would be appropriate despite negative troponin testing since polymorphic VT is frequently an ischemic rhythm. If the patient only had AF with aberrant conduction, increased metoprolol and initiation of an anticoagulation would be reasonable. EP study is not indicated. If the rhythm is identified as sustained symptomatic ventricular tachycardia in the presence of a structurally abnormal heart, the patient bears a class I indication for a defibrillator regardless of the outcome of EP study. Thiamine deficiency is common in individuals with chronic alcohol use disorder due to poor nutritional intake and impaired thiamine absorption. Immediate critical treatment for Wernicke's encephalopathy consists of high-dose intravenous thiamine to reverse the deficiency and prevent further neurological damage. The typical dose is 100 mg of thiamine administered intravenously. This should be given before glucose-containing fluids to avoid precipitating or worsening Wernicke's encephalopathy. Admission to the hospital is essential for close monitoring, administration of IV thiamine, and evaluation for other complications related to alcohol use, as well as to address any underlying medical issues. The patient has been tapered off ruxolitinib. You are considering adding on a second agent. Which of the following correctly describes the mechanism and pathophysiology underlying GVHD?
questions.stemHtml: A 45 year old male patient, who is 180 days post allogenic matched unrelated donor transplant for FLT3 – ITD NPM1 (wt) AML, and whose clinical course was complicated by acute GVHD requiring the use of methylprednisolone, and ruxolitinib, was referred for your opinion on progressive tightening of his skin, leading to uncomfortable flexion of his elbow, and not responding to steroids since 4 weeks. The patient has been tapered off ruxolitinib. You are considering adding on a second agent. Which of the following correctly describes the mechanism and pathophysiology underlying GVHD?

options.label: D
options.text: Combination T-cell and B-cell mediated response

questions.answerText: Combination T-cell and B-cell mediated response
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Combination T-cell and B-cell mediated response: T-cell mediated response correctly describes the mechanism and pathophysiology underlying graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). GVHD is a significant complication that can occur after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). It is characterized by donor T cells recognizing the recipient's tissues as foreign and mounting an immune response against them. This immune response is primarily mediated by T cells and is the central mechanism underlying GVHD. Here's a brief overview of the pathophysiology of GVHD: T-Cell Activation: In allogeneic HSCT, donor T cells are introduced into the recipient's body along with the transplanted hematopoietic stem cells. These donor T cells can recognize and react against the recipient's tissues, perceiving them as foreign. Donor T-Cell Response: Activated donor T cells proliferate and target recipient tissues, leading to a cascade of immune responses. They can directly damage recipient cells and also recruit other immune cells to amplify the response. Inflammatory Response: The immune response triggered by donor T cells can result in the release of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, leading to tissue damage and inflammation in various organs, including the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and liver. While B cells and natural killer (NK) cells can be involved in the overall immune response, the primary driver of GVHD pathophysiology is the T-cell mediated response. Therefore, therapies aimed at mitigating GVHD often focus on suppressing or modulating T-cell activity, such as through the use of immunosuppressive drugs like steroids and agents that target specific T-cell subsets. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Donor T-Cell Response: Activated donor T cells proliferate and target recipient tissues, leading to a cascade of immune responses. They can directly damage recipient cells and also recruit other immune cells to amplify the response.

Therefore, therapies aimed at mitigating GVHD often focus on suppressing or modulating T-cell activity, such as through the use of immunosuppressive drugs like steroids and agents that target specific T-cell subsets.

questions.solution: Correct Option C - HIV enzyme immunoassay (EIA) testing: This patient has oral hairy leukoplakia (OHL) based on physical examination and histological findings. OHL typically presents as a white patchy mucosal infiltrate that predominantly accumulates along the lateral tongue surface. It is thought to be secondary to active Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection. A biopsy typically shows severe hyperkeratosis (thickening of stratum corneum) and acanthosis (thickening of stratum basale/spinosum) with koilocytosis. Fungal elements such as hyphae are also seen but typically are unrelated etiologically. The presence of OHL should raise suspicion for an immunocompromised state such as HIV infection, warranting a screening assay. Enzyme immunoassay HIV-screening tests should be repeated if positive and confirmed via Western blot technique. Incorrect Options: Option A - Nystatin oral suspension 500,000 units four times daily: HIV EIA testing is necessary for this patient with OHL. Treatment of OHL requires correction of the underlying immunocompromised state. Nystatin oral suspension therapy is a treatment option for patients with oral candidiasis. Option B - Reassurance and monitoring: Although OHL has no risk of malignant transformation, simple monitoring would ignore the possibility of an underlying immunocompromised state in this patient. Option D - Oral acyclovir 400 mg orally every 4 hours: Oral acyclovir may result in a temporary resolution of OHL, but the lesions tend to reappear after treatment discontinuation. @Neet_pg_bot

What is the most common cause of a nodular infiltrates on a CT scan of the chest for a patient that is day 50 post – allogeneic transplant for high-risk AML?

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Aspergillosis: The most common cause of nodular infiltrates on a CT scan of the chest in a patient who is day 50 post-allogeneic transplant for high-risk AML is Aspergillosis. Patients who have undergone allogeneic stem cell transplantation, especially when they are immunocompromised due to the transplant and GVHD, are at increased risk of fungal infections. Aspergillosis, specifically invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA), is a common and serious fungal infection in this patient population. Aspergillus species, particularly Aspergillus fumigatus, are known pathogens that can cause invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in immunocompromised individuals. This infection often presents as nodular infiltrates on chest CT scans. Incorrect Options: Option B - Candida: While Candida species can cause fungal infections in immunocompromised patients, they are more commonly associated with bloodstream infections (candidemia) rather than pulmonary nodular infiltrates. Option C - Mucor: Mucormycosis (caused by Mucorales fungi) is another invasive fungal infection that can affect immunocompromised patients. It may present with pulmonary involvement, but nodular infiltrates are not as common as in aspergillosis. Option D - Staphylococcus aureus: Staphylococcus aureus is a bacterial pathogen that can cause various infections, including pneumonia, but it typically does not present with the characteristic nodular infiltrates seen in fungal infections like aspergillosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 63-year-old gentleman, ECOG 1, with h/o clear-cell renal cell carcinoma, post nephrectomy and metastectomy for an isolated liver lesion clinic and failed on 3 lines of therapy , including cabozantinib, nivolumab and axitinib, seeks your opinion regarding further management. His recent labs show a hgb of 9.9 g/dL as well as an LDH of 310 IU/L. You start the patient on 1.34 mg of tivozanib. Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is most likely to occur?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Hyponatremia: Tivozanib is a small molecule inhibitor of the VEGFR and was studied in a randomized, open label, multicenter trial versus sorafenib in patients with relapsed or refractory advanced renal cell carcinoma, who had received 2 or 3 prior systemic therapies. One of the agents had to be a VEGFR inhibitor. Patients were randomized to 1.34 mg once daily of Tivozanib on 21 out of 28 days or sorafenib 400 mg twice a day. Patients were treated until disease progression. The median progression free survival was 5.6 months versus 3.9 months. The hazard ratio was 0.73, 95% confidence interval 0.56–0.95, P = 0.016. The median overall survival was 16.4 versus 19.2 months, hazard ratio 0.97 . The objective response rate was 18% versus 8%. The most common adverse events included fatigue, diarrhea, hypertension and decreased appetite. The most common grade 3 or 4 laboratory abnormalities including hyponatremia, increased lipase and hypophosphatemia. The other electrolyte abnormalities (Hyperkalemia, Hypernatremia, Hypokalemia) are less likely to occur as primary side effects of tivozanib therapy, although they should still be monitored for as part of routine patient care. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Sarah is a 30-year-old female who presents to her primary care physician with shortness of breath and chest pain on exertion. She reports feeling fatigued lately and has a family history of heart disease. On physical examination, her blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, and her heart rate is 90 beats per minute. Auscultation of her heart reveals a harsh systolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border. An echocardiogram is ordered, which shows moderate aortic stenosis with a bicuspid aortic valve. What could be the most likely cause of Sarah's aortic stenosis?
questions.stemHtml: Sarah is a 30-year-old female who presents to her primary care physician with shortness of breath and chest pain on exertion. She reports feeling fatigued lately and has a family history of heart disease. On physical examination, her blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, and her heart rate is 90 beats per minute. Auscultation of her heart reveals a harsh systolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border. An echocardiogram is ordered, which shows moderate aortic stenosis with a bicuspid aortic valve. What could be the most likely cause of Sarah's aortic stenosis?
questions.solution: Option C - Bicuspid valve calcification A bicuspid aortic valve is a congenital cardiac defect in which the aortic valve has just two leaflets as opposed to three. The bicuspid aortic valve is a prevalent cause of aortic stenosis in young people. Exertional dyspnea, chest pain, exhaustion, and indicators of heart failure such as jugular venous distention and peripheral oedema are symptoms of aortic stenosis. A systolic ejection murmur is often heard best at the right upper sternal border during a physical examination. The diagnosis and degree of aortic stenosis are determined via an echocardiography. Currently, the most recommended treatment for moderate aortic stenosis is medical care to control symptoms. Surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement may be considered if aortic stenosis worsens or if medicinal therapy fails to adequately control symptoms. Incorrect Options: Option A - Rheumatic heart disease Rheumatic heart disease occurs when untreated streptococcal infection damages the heart valves, generally in youth. Although rheumatic heart disease can cause aortic stenosis, it is a relatively uncommon cause in developed countries and is more commonly associated with mitral valve disease. The scenario's physical examination findings, including a harsh systolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border, are more consistent with aortic stenosis caused by a bicuspid aortic valve. A history of prior streptococcal infection is generally required to diagnose rheumatic heart diseas e, and blood tests such as the antistreptolysin-O (ASO) titre may be needed to confirm the diagnosis. Antibiotics are often prescribed to treat the streptococcal infection underlying rheumatic heart disease, as well as drugs to control symptoms and prevent complications. In severe circumstances, valve repair or replacement may be essential. Option B - Age related aortic stenosis Age-related aortic stenosis is a form of aortic stenosis caused by degeneration and calcification of the aortic valve in the elderly. This kind of aortic stenosis typically affects adults over the age of 65 and is more prevalent in males than in women . Senile degenerative aortic stenosis can produce dyspnea on exercise, chest pain, and weariness, but it is not the most common cause of aortic stenosis in a 30-year-old. The scenario's physical examination results, particularly a strong systolic murmur heard most prominently at the right upper sternal border, are more consistent with aortic stenosis induced by a bicuspid aortic valve. Medications are commonly used to treat senile degenerative aortic stenosis in order to manage symptoms and prevent consequences, such as heart failure and arrhythmias. In severe circumstances, it may be required to replace the valve. The scenario's physical examination results, particularly a strong systolic murmur heard most prominently at the right upper sternal border, are more consistent with aortic stenosis induced by a bicuspid aortic valve. The bicuspid aortic valve is a congenital heart anomaly in which the aortic valve has two leaflets instead of three and is a prevalent cause of aortic stenosis in young adults. Medication is often used to treat aortic stenosis caused by a bicuspid aortic valve in order to reduce symptoms and prevent consequences, such as heart failure or arrhythmias. questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with hypertension and palpitations and is diagnosed with a paraganglioma. With which of the following mutations are paragangliomas associated ?
questions.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman presents with hypertension and palpitations and is diagnosed with a paraganglioma. With which of the following mutations are paragangliomas associated ?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - VHL mutation: Hereditary catecholamine producing intra or extra-adrenal paragangliomas can be caused by one of the following germline mutations: RET proto-oncogene von Hippel-Lindau gene (vHL) Neurofibromatosis Type 1 gene (NF-1) Succinate dehydrogenase subunit B (SDHB) Succinate dehydrogenase subunit D (SDHB) Patients with SDHB or SDHD are more likely to present with extra-adrenal disease, bilateral tumours and metastatic disease. According to the guidelines issued by The First International Symposium on Phaeochromocytomas (October 2005), genetic screening should be individualised and is generally warranted in: Patients aged < 50 years, presenting with catecholamine secreting Multiple tumours Malignant tumours Bilateral tumours Incorrect Options: Option A - 21-Hydroxylase deficiency: It is associated with adrenal insufficiency Option C - MENIN mutation: It is associated with MEN syndrome Option D - HRPT 2 mutation: It is associated with HPT jaw tumor syndrome @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option B - VHL mutation:

  • Hereditary catecholamine producing intra or extra-adrenal paragangliomas can be caused by one of the following germline mutations:
    • RET proto-oncogene
    • von Hippel-Lindau gene (vHL)
    • Neurofibromatosis Type 1 gene (NF-1)
    • Succinate dehydrogenase subunit B (SDHB)
    • Succinate dehydrogenase subunit D (SDHB)
  • Patients with SDHB or SDHD are more likely to present with extra-adrenal disease, bilateral tumours and metastatic disease. According to the guidelines issued by The First International Symposium on Phaeochromocytomas (October 2005), genetic screening should be individualised and is generally warranted in:
    • Patients aged < 50 years, presenting with catecholamine secreting
    • Multiple tumours
    • Malignant tumours
    • Bilateral tumours

 

Incorrect Options:

Option A - 21-Hydroxylase deficiency: It is associated with adrenal insufficiency

Option C - MENIN mutation: It is associated with MEN syndrome

Option D - HRPT 2 mutation: It is associated with HPT jaw tumor syndrome

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Carney complex: Carney complex (CNC) is an autosomal dominant disorder and affects multiple glands in the body, such as the thyroid, pituitary, and adrenal glands. Carney complex is also known to cause cardiac myxomas, abnormal pigmentation (lentiginosis) or myxomas of the skin, breast myxomatosis, melanotic schwannoma, and endocrine tumours, such as large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumour, thyroid adenoma, GH/PRL-secreting pituitary adenoma and ovarian cysts. The most common endocrine manifestation is primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease (PPNAD) which can be micro or macronodular causing Cushing’s syndrome. Approximately 25% of cases occur sporadically, as a result of a de novo mutation. An inactivating mutation of the PRKAR1A gene can be identified in two-thirds of patients. Inactivating mutations of phosphodiesterase genes PDE11A and more rarely PDE8B have also been observed in patients with isolated micronodular pigmented (PPNAD) or non-pigmented hyperplasia. A clinical diagnosis is made by finding two of the clinical features or one of the features either an affected first-degree relative or mutation in PRKAR1A gene. Incorrect Options: Option B - Cowden syndrome: Cowden syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition caused by an inactivating mutation in the PTEN tumour suppressor gene. It is characterised by multiple hamartomas involving skin and mucosa such as facial papules, acral keratosis or palmoplantar keratosis involving palms and feet and oral papillomatosis. Thyroid abnormalities are present in >75%, commonly follicular thyroid cancer, multinodular goitre or thyroid adenoma. Other non-cutaneous features are fibrocystic breast disease, ovarian cyst, gastrointestinal polyps, bone cysts, haematoma of cerebellum (Lhermitte-Duclos disease), lipomas and macrocephaly. Option C - McCune-Albright syndrome: McCune-Albright syndrome is a genetic condition due to GNAS-1 gene mutation and is characterised by polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, unilateral café-au-lait spots, precocious puberty and ACTH independent Cushing’s with bilateral macronodular hyperplasia. questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option A - Carney complex:

  • Carney complex (CNC) is an autosomal dominant disorder and affects multiple glands in the body, such as the thyroid, pituitary, and adrenal glands.
  • Carney complex is also known to cause cardiac myxomas, abnormal pigmentation (lentiginosis) or myxomas of the skin, breast myxomatosis, melanotic schwannoma, and endocrine tumours, such as large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumour, thyroid adenoma, GH/PRL-secreting pituitary adenoma and ovarian cysts.
  • The most common endocrine manifestation is primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease (PPNAD) which can be micro or macronodular causing Cushing’s syndrome.
  • Approximately 25% of cases occur sporadically, as a result of a de novo mutation. An inactivating mutation of the PRKAR1A gene can be identified in two-thirds of patients. Inactivating mutations of phosphodiesterase genes PDE11A and more rarely PDE8B have also been observed in patients with isolated micronodular pigmented (PPNAD) or non-pigmented hyperplasia.

It is characterised by multiple hamartomas involving skin and mucosa such as facial papules, acral keratosis or palmoplantar keratosis involving palms and feet and oral papillomatosis. Thyroid abnormalities are present in >75%, commonly follicular thyroid cancer, multinodular goitre or thyroid adenoma. Other non-cutaneous features are fibrocystic breast disease, ovarian cyst, gastrointestinal polyps, bone cysts, haematoma of cerebellum (Lhermitte-Duclos disease), lipomas and macrocephaly.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about the use of topiramate for migraine prevention?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is true about the use of topiramate for migraine prevention?

options.label: B
options.text: It reduces the serum concentrations of estrogen and can lead to contraceptive failure at lower doses (<100 mg per day)

options.label: C
options.text: It is associated with an increased risk for nephrolithiasis

questions.answerText: It is associated with an increased risk for nephrolithiasis
questions.solution: Correct Option C - It is associated with an increased risk for nephrolithiasis: Use of topiramate is associated with an increased rate of kidney stones, especially calcium phosphate stones. In clinical trials the incidence was 1% at 100 mg and 2% at 200 mg compared to 0% in the placebo group. This risk is related to the fact that topiramate causes metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, hyperuricemia and decreased urinary citrate which promotes renal stone formation. The development of renal stones may be a late adverse effect of treatment. Good hydration, and lower daily dose may reduce the risk. Incorrect Options: Option A - It is pregnancy category B: Topiramate has been recently labeled by the FDA as pregnancy category D based on evidence showing a two-fold increase in cleft lip and less often cleft palate when used during pregnancy. Option B - It reduces the serum concentrations of estrogen and can lead to contraceptive failure at lower doses (<100 mg per day): At doses above 200 mg per day, there may be a dose related decrease in plasma concentrations of estrogens and progestins in patients taking birth control pills. Lower doses of topiramate don’t seem to affect the efficacy of oral contraceptives. Option D - It causes weight gain: In contrast to many other migraine preventive medications, topiramate has been associated with anorexia and weight loss in clinical trials which in certain patients can be a desirable side effect. Option E - The combination of topiramate with propranolol has been shown to be more effective than either drug alone in migraine prevention: In a clinical trial the combination of topiramate and propranolol offered no benefit over topiramate alone for migraine prevention. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 47-year-old gentleman, with alcohol related liver disease, admitted with esophageal variceal bleeding, undergoes successful ligation and therapy with octreotide. His hemoglobin has been stable over the last 48 hours. However, his abdominal imaging, showed pancreatitis with splanchnic vein thrombosis. You plan anticoagulation. Which of the following benefits can be seen compared to observation when providing anticoagulation to patients with splanchnic vein thrombosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 47-year-old gentleman, with alcohol related liver disease, admitted with esophageal variceal bleeding, undergoes successful ligation and therapy with octreotide. His hemoglobin has been stable over the last 48 hours. However, his abdominal imaging, showed pancreatitis with splanchnic vein thrombosis. You plan anticoagulation. Which of the following benefits can be seen compared to observation when providing anticoagulation to patients with splanchnic vein thrombosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced SVT progression, Improvement in overall mortality

options.label: C
options.text: Reduced incidence of recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE)

questions.solution: Correct Option D - All the above: In a recent systemic review with a meta-analysis, as reviewed here, with the article linked below, the utilization of anticoagulation in patients with splanchnic vein thrombosis, has been shown to improve recanalization, minimize progression, minimize recurrent venous thromboembolism, and improve overall mortality, but at the expense of increased hemorrhage. In the journal Blood on March 4, 2021, investigators report on anticoagulation therapy for splanchnic vein thrombosis per systematic review and meta-analysis. To date, there has been little data supporting the standard treatment approach for splanchnic vein thrombosis. A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted to help determine not only the efficacy but also the safety of anticoagulation for splenic vein thrombosis. Medline, EMBase, and clinical trials.gov were searched from inception through December 2019. Observational studies and randomized control trials were included. The pooled proportion and risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals and calculated in a random-effects model. 4,312 records were identified. 97 studies including 7,969 patients were analyzed. In patients receiving anticoagulation, the rates of splanchnic vein thrombosis recanalization, progression, recurrent venous thromboembolism, major bleeding and overall mortality were reported as 85% (95% confidence interval, 51–64), 5% (CI 3–7), 11% (CI 8–15), 9% (CI 7–12) and 11% (CI 9–14), respectively. Patient’s not receiving anticoagulation had 22% (95% CI 15–31), 15% (CI 8–27), 14% (CI 9–21), 16% (CI 13–20), and 25% (CI 20–31), respectively. Compared to observation rather than treatment, anticoagulation therapy obtained higher recanalization rates, relative risk, 2.39, 95% confidence interval 1.66–3.44. Lower thrombosis progression was also observed, relative risk, 0.24, 95% confidence interval 0.13–0.42. The same trend was seen with major bleeding, relative risk 0.73, 95% confidence interval 0.58–0.92. With regards to overall mortality, the relative risk was 0.45, 95% confidence interval, 0.33–0.60). The authors concluded “these results demonstrate that anticoagulant therapy improves splanchnic vein thrombosis recanalization and reduces the risk of thrombosis progression without increasing major bleeding. The incidence of recurrent venous thromboembolism remains substantial in patients receiving anticoagulation as well. Effects were consistent across the different subgroups of patients.” @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old female with a history of stage 4 CKD presents to the emergency department complaining of muscle weakness and nausea. Laboratory investigations reveal a serum potassium level of 6.5 mEq/L. Which of the following is the initial treatment for hyperkalemia in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Calcium gluconate Hyperkalemia is a common chronic kidney disease (CKD) complication and can be life-threatening if left untreated. In patients with severe hyperkalemia (potassium > 6.5 mEq/L), immediate treatment is required to prevent cardiac arrhythmias and other complications. One of the initial treatments for hyperkalemia in CKD patients is the administration of calcium gluconate. Calcium gluconate works by stabilizing the cardiac membrane potential, which helps to prevent or treat the arrhythmias that can occur with hyperkalemia. It does not lower the potassium level itself; rather, it protects the heart from the effects of high potassium levels. Calcium can also help counteract hyperkalemia's potential adverse effects on neuromuscular and gastrointestinal function. Calcium gluconate is typically administered intravenously, with the dose depending on the severity of hyperkalemia and the patient's underlying medical conditions. In patients with CKD, the dose may need to be adjusted based on the patient's renal function, as high doses of calcium can cause hypercalcemia, leading to other complications. It is important to note that calcium gluconate is not a definitive treatment for hyperkalemia in CKD patients. Other interventions, such as insulin and glucose administration, diuretics, or dialysis, should be followed to lower the serum potassium level. Incorrect options: Option B: Insulin and glucose Insulin and glucose can shift potassium from the extracellular space to the intracellular space, but they should only be given after calcium gluconate administration. Option C: Kayexalate Kayexalate is an ion-exchange resin that binds with potassium in the gut and increases its excretion, but its onset of action is slow and may take several hours. Option D: Furosemide Furosemide can be used to increase potassium excretion but is not effective in patients with severe renal impairment. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - There is no difference in outcomes between patients who achieve a CR following one cycle of induction therapy vs. two cycles of induction therapy if a CR is obtained following treatment In younger patients with AML (generally considered less than 55-60 years old) two phases of chemotherapy are generally administered: First, the induction phase with the goal to be described below and second, the consolidation phase, consisting of multiple courses of chemotherapy and/or hematopoietic cell transplanation (HCT). The primary goal of induction chemotherapy is to enable the body's bone marrow to function properly by removing malignant cells. Numerically, the goal is to decrease the total leukemic cell burden to less than 10 9 cells, as this is the level of cells that can be detected by current laboratory techniques. When patients achieve this bench mark, the underlying assumption is that residual disease remaining is not able to be cytologically detected and thus is classified as minimal residual disease that requires additional therapy (consolidation chemotherapy or HCT) to be of curative intent. The current NCCN guidelines list the following induction regimen as their category 1 recommendation for induction therapy in patients under the age of 60: Standard dose cytarabine 100-200 mg/m2 continuous infusion x 7 days with idarubicin 12 mg/m2 or daunorubicin 60-90 mg/m2 x 3 days. (7+3 therapy) Following completion of induction therapy a unilateral bone marrow biopsy is obtained to assess response to therapy. This is typically done on day 7 following completion of induction chemotherapy, or 12-21 days after the start of treatment. If greater than 5% leukemic blasts are found on BMB, the NCCN recommendations is an additional cycle of induction chemotherapy. In a report published by Rowe et al. Cancer 2010, they found that among patients enrolled in Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) studies between 1983 to 1993, that long-term outcome was similar for patients who required 1 or 2 cycles of induction therapy to achieve CR, and their outcome was independent of other prognostic variables, such as age or karyotype. @Neet_pg_bot

Research has indicated that rituximab can induce remission in people with Anti-GBM Disease who have not responded to initial treatment with plasma exchange and steroids. Rituximab is generally well-tolerated, with infusion responses being the most common adverse effect, and it has a lower chance of generating infections and other problems than Cyclophosphamide. However, Cyclophosphamide has more side effects than rituximab and is generally reserved for patients who cannot tolerate or have not responded to rituximab therapy. Improved Overall and Progression-Free Survival (PFS): Chemoradiation therapy not only improves overall survival but also progression-free survival. This means that patients are less likely to experience disease progression or recurrence when chemotherapy is added to radiation therapy. By adding chemotherapy to radiation, it not only reduces the risk of local disease progression but also decreases the likelihood of distant metastases, which is particularly relevant in NPC as it has a propensity for distant spread. questions.solution: ng>: Carotid duplex ultrasonography is typically used to assess carotid artery disease and may not provide immediate information needed for acute stroke management. It focuses on the carotid arteries and their role in stroke risk but may not reveal information about the extent of the current brain ischemia. Cerebral catheter angiography (C) : Cerebral catheter angiography is an invasive procedure and is not typically the immediate next step in acute stroke management. It is reserved for specific cases when CT or MRI findings are inconclusive or when endovascular intervention is being considered. It is not the primary diagnostic tool for assessing acute stroke. Brain MRI (D) : While brain MRI is valuable for assessing stroke, it may not be the immediate next step in acute management. MRI can provide more detailed information about the extent and type of ischemic injury but can take longer to perform compared to CT perfusion. Transcranial Doppler (E) : Transcranial Doppler is used to assess blood flow velocities in the intracranial arteries and is often used to monitor cerebral blood flow during and after interventions but may not provide the comprehensive information needed for acute stroke management. CT perfusion scan (A) : A CT perfusion scan provides crucial information about the extent of ischemic injury, the presence of salvageable tissue (penumbra), and can help guide decisions regarding thrombolytic therapy (if within the time window) or endovascular intervention. It can quickly assess tissue viability and help identify patients who may benefit from reperfusion therapies. In this case, the CT perfusion scan can help determine the extent of the ischemic injury, the presence of salvageable tissue, and whether the patient is a candidate for thrombolytic therapy or other interventions. Time is critical in stroke management, and this investigation can provide valuable information for making timely treatment decisions. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 64-year-old male with a history of AML, now in remission after an allogenic SCT is admitted for encephalopathy. Initial lab work up reveals thrombocytopenia and transaminitis. Perianal ulcers are noted on exam. HSV and VZV swabs are negative. Confirmatory diagnostic testing is performed and reveals the diagnosis. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.stemHtml: A 64-year-old male with a history of AML, now in remission after an allogenic SCT is admitted for encephalopathy. Initial lab work up reveals thrombocytopenia and transaminitis. Perianal ulcers are noted on exam. HSV and VZV swabs are negative. Confirmatory diagnostic testing is performed and reveals the diagnosis. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - IV Ganciclovir The patients presentation is consistent with cutaneous CMV. Cutaneous CMV should be considered in immunosuppressed patients presenting with ulcers, particularly ulcers that do not respond to standard therapy. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a double-stranded DNA virus that is a member of the Herpesviridae family. In immunocompetent hosts, primary CMV infections often go unnoticed. CMV can establish latency and reactivate during times of stress and immunosuppression. CMV has broad clinical manifestations and can affect multiple organ systems including: Skin (cutaneous lesions/ulcers) Hepatic (manifesting as transaminitis) Hematologic (manifesting as leukopenia) Gastrointestinal Neurologic (encephalopathy) Ocular (CMV retinitis) Pulmonary Overall, cutaneous CMV is rare. The dermis is relatively inhospitable to CMV, so cutaneous CMV is usually seen in immunocompromised patients with disseminated disease. Cutaneous CMV most commonly presents as ulcers with a preferential location for the perianal area, which is thought to be due to viral shedding form the gastrointestinal tract. The gold standard for diagnosis of cutaneous CMV is a biopsy which reveals basophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies . IHC staining for CMV can confirm the diagnosis. For CMV viremia, the diagnosis can be made with serologic testing: PCR for viral load or CMV pp65 antigenemia testing. First-line treatment for CMV is IV Ganciclovir. CMV can also be treated with Valganciclovir, Cidofovir, or Foscarnet. Acyclovir must be phosphorylated by viral-encoded thymidine kinase to its active form. Unlike HSV and VZV, CMV does not encode a thymidine kinase so acyclovir is not an approved treatment for CMV. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male patient with long-standing chronic kidney disease presents with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Laboratory tests show a serum calcium level of 12.0 mg/dL (normal range: 8.5-10.2 mg/dL), serum phosphorus level of 5.0 mg/dL (normal range: 2.5-4.5 mg/dL), and a high parathyroid hormone (PTH) level. What is the most likely cause of hypercalcemia in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male patient with long-standing chronic kidney disease presents with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Laboratory tests show a serum calcium level of 12.0 mg/dL (normal range: 8.5-10.2 mg/dL), serum phosphorus level of 5.0 mg/dL (normal range: 2.5-4.5 mg/dL), and a high parathyroid hormone (PTH) level. What is the most likely cause of hypercalcemia in this patient?

options.label: B
options.text: Increased calcium absorption from the gut

options.label: D
options.text: Decreased expression of calcium-sensing receptors in the parathyroid

questions.answerText: Decreased expression of calcium-sensing receptors in the parathyroid
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Decreased expression of calcium-sensing receptors in the parathyroid Pathophysiology: In chronic kidney disease, the kidneys cannot excrete phosphate effectively, leading to hyperphosphatemia, and low serum calcitriol causes a decrease in serum calcium. High levels of serum phosphorus and low calcium stimulate the secretion of PTH from the parathyroid gland causing secondary hyperparathyroidism. PTH increases serum calcium concentration by increasing calcium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the nephron and indirectly increasing bone reabsorption. In long-standing CKD, some patients develop persistent hyperfunction of the parathyroid, which is called tertiary hyperparathyroidism. This disorder develops due to increased parenchymal mass and cellular differentiation of the parathyroid gland. These changes in the parathyroid gland result in decreased expression of calcium-sensing receptors and abnormalities in vitamin D receptors, leading to further secretion of PTH. This autonomous production of PTH results in hypercalcemia. Patients often have serum PTH levels >800 pg/mL. Clinical features: Hypercalcemia can cause abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, fatigue, and confusion. Management: Treatment for hypercalcemia in chronic kidney disease includes managing hyperphosphatemia with phosphate binders, controlling secondary hyperparathyroidism with calcimimetics or vitamin D analogs, and treating the underlying cause if applicable. Incorrect options: Option A: Excessive calcium intake: Excessive calcium intake can cause hypercalcemia, but it is unlikely to be the cause, as the patient has hyperparathyroidism . Excess calcium intake would lower parathyroid hormone levels. Option B: Increased calcium absorption from the gut: Increased calcium absorption from the gut can cause hypercalcemia. Still, it is unlikely to be the cause, as the patient has chronic kidney disease and cannot produce calcitriol, essential for calcium absorption. Option C: High serum phosphorus levels : High serum phosphorus levels are in response to chronic kidney disease . As kidney function declines, the kidney can no longer respond to PTH or FGF-23, and serum phosphate levels continue to increase. @Neet_pg_bot

    • In long-standing CKD, some patients develop persistent hyperfunction of the parathyroid, which is called tertiary hyperparathyroidism. This disorder develops due to increased parenchymal mass and cellular differentiation of the parathyroid gland.
    • These changes in the parathyroid gland result in decreased expression of calcium-sensing receptors and abnormalities in vitamin D receptors, leading to further secretion of PTH. This autonomous production of PTH results in hypercalcemia. Patients often have serum PTH levels >800 pg/mL.
  • Clinical features: Hypercalcemia can cause abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, fatigue, and confusion.
  • Management: Treatment for hypercalcemia in chronic kidney disease includes managing hyperphosphatemia with phosphate binders, controlling secondary hyperparathyroidism with calcimimetics or vitamin D analogs, and treating the underlying cause if applicable.

Incorrect options:

Option A: Excessive calcium intake:

  • Excessive calcium intake can cause hypercalcemia, but it is unlikely to be the cause, as the patient has hyperparathyroidism. Excess calcium intake would lower parathyroid hormone levels.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Labs reveal blood glucose of 460 mg/dL, pH of 7.20, and potassium of 2.2 mEq/L. Urinalysis is positive for ketones. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Labs reveal blood glucose of 460 mg/dL, pH of 7.20, and potassium of 2.2 mEq/L. Urinalysis is positive for ketones. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Administer 0.45% NaCl infusion: This is the correct initial intervention. The patient is presenting with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which is characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. The low blood pH (7.20) indicates acidosis. The patient's low potassium level (2.2 mEq/L) suggests hypokalemia, likely due to intracellular shifts of potassium as a result of acidosis. Administering a 0.45% NaCl (normal saline) infusion helps to correct dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and acidosis. It also assists in improving tissue perfusion. After initiating fluid resuscitation, insulin administration can be started to help lower blood glucose levels and further correct acidosis Incorrect Options: Option B - Administer potassium chloride: While hypokalemia (low potassium) is a potential complication of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), administering potassium chloride as the initial intervention can be dangerous. The patient's potassium level is already low (2.2 mEq/L), and administering potassium without proper fluid resuscitation can lead to further imbalances and potentially life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Correcting fluid balance is the priority before addressing potassium imbalances. Option C - Administer 0.1 units/kg IV insulin: While insulin administration is a crucial component of DKA treatment, it should not be the initial step in this case. Before insulin is administered, it's important to address the patient's fluid and electrolyte imbalances. Administering insulin without adequate hydration can lead to further decreases in potassium levels and potential complications. Option D - Administer a dextrose solution: Administering a dextrose solution is not appropriate as the initial intervention for DKA. The patient's blood glucose level is already very high (460 mg/dL), and giving more glucose can exacerbate the hyperglycemia and worsen the acidosis. The primary concern in DKA management is first addressing fluid and electrolyte imbalances. @Neet_pg_bot

Chest x-ray reveals parenchymal infiltrates in the lower lobes of the lung. A high-resolution CT scan shows ground-glass opacities and calcified pleural plaques. questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old shipbuilding industry worker presents to the clinic complaining of dyspnea and a non-productive cough for the last two months. Chest x-ray reveals parenchymal infiltrates in the lower lobes of the lung. A high-resolution CT scan shows ground-glass opacities and calcified pleural plaques. Exposure to which of the following substance is responsible for this pathology?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Asbestos: Ground-glass opacities, calcified pleural plaques, and a history of working in shipbuilding suggest a diagnosis of asbestosis. Asbestosis is an interstitial lung disease caused by the inhalation of asbestos fibers. Individuals working in shipbuilding, insulation, roofing, mining, and firefighting equipment manufacturing industries are at risk of inhaling asbestos fibres. Asbestosis develops slowly over time. The clinical features of asbestosis may not become apparent until 15-20 years or more after the initial exposure to asbestos fibers. Clinical features of asbestosis include the following: Dry cough Dyspnea Weight loss Clubbing Diagnosis of asbestosis is based on the following tests: Pulmonary function test (PFT): Restrictive pattern (decreased FEV1 and normal or increased FEV1/FVC) would be seen on PFTs. Chest x-ray: Parenchymal infiltrates in the lower lobes of the lungs and pleural plaques can be seen on the chest x-ray. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT): HRCT is a more sensitive imaging test than a chest x-ray for diagnosing asbestosis. Ground-glass opacities, pleural thickening, and calcified pleural plaques (shown below) would be seen on HRCT. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Alveolar sputum samples obtained using BAL would show the presence of asbestos bodies, which are golden-brown, rod-shaped structures. Asbestos bodies are indicative of asbestos exposure. Incorrect Options: Option A - Coal dust: Exposure to coal dust can cause coal worker’s pneumoconiosis (CWP). CWP is characterised by the accumulation of coal dust particles in the lungs, which can lead to inflammation and fibrosis. Symptoms of CWP include shortness of breath, coughing, and chest tightness. Chest x-rays may show small nodules in the upper lobes of the lung. However, the presence of calcified pleural plaques is not a typical feature of CWP. Option C - Silica dust: Silica exposure can occur in people working in sandblasting, ceramics, and foundries. Symptoms of silicosis include shortness of breath, coughing, and chest pain. Chest X-rays may show small nodules in the lung tissue, while high-resolution CT scans may reveal ground-glass opacities. However, calcified pleural plaques are not seen in silicosis. Option D - Mouldy hay: Exposure to mouldy hay can cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis, an immune reaction to organic antigens. Chest x-rays may show diffuse patchy infiltrates in the lung tissue. However, calcified pleural plaques are not found in hypersensitivity pneumonitis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Chronic phase, accelerated phase, blast crisis and Ph+ ALL
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Chronic phase, accelerated phase, blast crisis, and Ph+ ALL: The PACE trial (Ponatinib Ph+ ALL and CML Evaluation) was a pivotal clinical trial that led to the approval of ponatinib (trade name: Iclusig) for the treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph+ ALL). This trial included a broad spectrum of patients with different phases of CML and Ph+ ALL, as follows: Chronic phase: Patients in the chronic phase of CML, similar to the case scenario described. Accelerated phase: Patients in the accelerated phase of CML, characterized by more aggressive disease features. Blast crisis: Patients in the blast crisis phase of CML, which is the most advanced and aggressive phase. Ph+ ALL: Patients with Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Ponatinib was studied and ultimately approved for patients who had resistance or intolerance to other tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), including those who had progressed through multiple lines of TKI therapy. Therefore, the PACE trial included a wide range of patients in different disease phases to assess the efficacy and safety of ponatinib in this population. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option B - Chronic phase, accelerated phase, blast crisis, and Ph+ ALL:

The PACE trial (Ponatinib Ph+ ALL and CML Evaluation) was a pivotal clinical trial that led to the approval of ponatinib (trade name: Iclusig) for the treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph+ ALL). This trial included a broad spectrum of patients with different phases of CML and Ph+ ALL, as follows:

  • Chronic phase: Patients in the chronic phase of CML, similar to the case scenario described.
  • Accelerated phase: Patients in the accelerated phase of CML, characterized by more aggressive disease features.
  • Blast crisis: Patients in the blast crisis phase of CML, which is the most advanced and aggressive phase.
  • Ph+ ALL: Patients with Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

Ponatinib was studied and ultimately approved for patients who had resistance or intolerance to other tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), including those who had progressed through multiple lines of TKI therapy. Therefore, the PACE trial included a wide range of patients in different disease phases to assess the efficacy and safety of ponatinib in this population.

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Significant bilateral renal artery stenosis: In bilateral renal artery stenosis, GFR is preserved by the actions of angiotensin II, afferent arteriolar vasodilation, and efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. options.label: A
options.text: There is no sex-based difference in the incidence of thyroid disease in FAP.

options.label: B
options.text: Up to 15% of thyroid nodules seen in FAP can contain foci of cancer.

options.label: C
options.text: When compared to men with FAP, women with FAP have an increased incidence of benign thyroid disease.

options.label: D
options.text: Patients with FAP should undergo thyroid cancer surveillance with thyroid ultrasound every 2 to 3 years.

questions.answerText: When compared to men with FAP, women with FAP have an increased incidence of benign thyroid disease.
questions.solution: Correct Option C - When compared to men with FAP, women with FAP have an increased incidence of benign thyroid disease. Studies have found that in general, women with FAP have a higher incidence of papillary thyroid cancers as well as benign thyroid disease. One particular study found that women have a 11.1% incidence of thyroid cancer compared to 0% in men. The same group also found that women with FAP have a nearly 17% incidence of benign thyroid disease and an overall incidence of thyroid disease that was approximately 9% due to no thyroid disease being noted in men with FAP. While as many as 38% of patients with FAP may have thyroid nodules, it is unknown how many harbor foci of cancer. Additionally, the rate at which benign thyroid nodules progress to cancer is also unknown. Studies have found that the mean age for the development of thyroid cancer in patients with FAP is around 28 years old (range: 12-62 years old). Because of this, the American College of Gastroenterology recommends starting yearly screening with thyroid ultrasound when FAP patients are teenagers. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man is diagnosed with left-sided colon cancer. Which of the following methods is best for determining if he has Lynch syndrome?
questions.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man is diagnosed with left-sided colon cancer. Which of the following methods is best for determining if he has Lynch syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Thorough family history looking for colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer, or other Lynch-related malignancies

options.label: D
options.text: Careful evaluation of histologic features of tumors under microscopy

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Immunochemistry testing of the tumor A recent study compared the sensitivity of Bethesda criteria and Amsterdam criteria to immunochemistry testing. In tumors demonstrating a loss of mismatch repair proteins on immunochemistry staining, up to 13% of Lynch-associated tumors were missed using Bethesda criteria to identify associated histologic features. Although some of the patients met the Amsterdam criteria for Lynch syndrome, not all of the missed patients did. Thus, immunochemistry staining is recommended for all tumors, as it can determine further surveillance for both patients and their families and help guide therapy for the cancer patient. Incorrect Options: Option A - Thorough family history looking for colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer, or other Lynch-related malignancies While a thorough family history is important in identifying individuals at risk for Lynch syndrome, it alone is not sufficient for confirming the diagnosis. Lynch syndrome can have variable penetrance, and some cases may not have a strong family history of the syndrome. Option B - Genetic testing Genetic testing for Lynch syndrome is important for confirming the diagnosis, but it is often performed after identifying potential cases through tumor testing. Immunochemistry testing of the tumor is a common initial step before considering genetic testing. Option D - Careful evaluation of histologic features of tumors under microscopy Histologic features of tumors, such as the presence of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and a Crohn's-like lymphocytic reaction, can provide clues to Lynch syndrome, but they are not definitive for diagnosis. Immunochemistry testing is a more direct method to assess MMR protein expression and microsatellite instability in the tumor tissue. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Primary progressive multiple sclerosis: The most consistent diagnosis with this presentation is Primary progressive multiple sclerosis (PPMS). Let's break down the key features of this case: Progressive Gait Difficulties: The patient has been experiencing progressive gait difficulties for 2 years. This points toward a chronic and progressive neurological disorder. Neurological Exam Findings: Bilateral lower extremity spasticity, worse on the right. Brisk reflexes. Upgoing toes and clonus on both sides. Bilateral lower extremity weakness, affecting flexor more than extensor muscle groups. Decreased proprioception in the feet. These clinical findings are indicative of upper motor neuron dysfunction, which is a characteristic feature of multiple sclerosis. Imaging Findings: Brain MRI shows demyelinating lesions consistent with multiple sclerosis. Spinal cord MRI reveals multiple short segment T2 lesions without enhancement. These findings are also consistent with multiple sclerosis. Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Analysis: Normal glucose and protein levels in the CSF. Elevated IgG index and the presence of oligoclonal bands in the CSF but not in the serum. These findings are suggestive of intrathecal antibody production, which is seen in multiple sclerosis. Based on the clinical presentation, imaging findings, and CSF analysis, this patient meets the criteria for a diagnosis of Primary Progressive Multiple Sclerosis (PPMS). PPMS is characterized by a gradual progression of symptoms from the onset, and it typically presents with features of upper motor neuron involvement, as seen in this case. Incorrect Options: Option A - Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS): This form of MS is characterized by relapses and remissions of neurological symptoms, which is not consistent with the progressive nature of this case. Option B - Secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (SPMS): SPMS typically follows an initial relapsing-remitting course and then transitions into a progressive phase. This patient's presentation appears to be primarily progressive from the beginning, so SPMS is less likely. Option D - Clinically isolated syndrome (CIS): CIS refers to a single episode of neurological symptoms that may or may not progress to definite multiple sclerosis. This patient's symptoms have been progressive for 2 years, making CIS less likely. Option E - Neuromyelitis optica (NMO): NMO is characterized by optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis. The imaging findings in this case are more consistent with multiple sclerosis rather than NMO. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: A
options.text: Expectant management is appropriate for women with AFLP without jaundice or coagulation abnormalities.

options.label: B
options.text: UDCA shows no evidence of improving fetal outcomes in women with intrahepatic cholestasis.

options.text: Women with hepatitis C should be treated to decrease the risk of vertical transmission.

questions.answerText: All pregnant women should be screened for hepatitis C virus infection.
questions.solution: Correct Option D - All pregnant women should be screened for hepatitis C virus infection. In 2018, the Infectious Disease Society of America and the AASLD recommended universal hepatitis C screening in pregnancy. Incorrect Options: Option A - Expectant management is appropriate for women with AFLP without jaundice or coagulation abnormalities. Women with AFLP should undergo delivery promptly. Women affected by AFLP and their offspring should be tested for long-chain 3 hydroxyacyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency. The offspring should also be monitored for manifestations of LCHCAD deficiency, which include hypoketotic hypoglycemia and fatty liver. Coagulopathy and hyperbilirubinemia are common but not universal, and delivery is still indicated in all cases. Option B - UDCA shows no evidence of improving fetal outcomes in women with intrahepatic cholestasis. UDCA normalizes bile acid patterns in fetuses with minimal amniotic fluid and cord blood accumulation. One meta-analysis showed it was associated with less pruritus, improved liver enzymes, and possibly improved fetal outcomes. Option C - Women with hepatitis C should be treated to decrease the risk of vertical transmission. Treatment for HCV should not be offered to pregnant women to treat HCV or to decrease the risk of vertical transmission. HCV presents little risk to mother or infant during pregnancy since a state of relative immune suppression occurs. Aminotransferase levels decrease in the second and third trimester. There is a 3-10% risk of vertical transmission at delivery. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: B

options.text: A 72-year-old male with lung metastases and history of kidney transplant on immunosuppression

questions.solution: Correct Option C - A 72-year-old male with lung metastases and history of kidney transplant on immunosuppression: Of the listed patients, the 72-year-old male with lung metastases and history of kidney transplant on immunosuppression is the one who is NOT a candidate for treatment with Cemiplimab. Cemiplimab is a potent, high-affinity human monoclonal antibody directed against programmed death 1 (PD-1). It is used in the management of lung cancer, multiple myeloma, and squamous cell carcinoma of the skin. PD-1 is expressed on the surface of activated T-cells, B-cells, and myeloid cells. When programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) binds to PD-1, it delivers a signal to inhibit T-cell proliferation. By binding to PD-1, pembrolizumab prevents tumour cell PD-L1 from binding to it, allowing the immune system to target and destroy the malignant cells. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved cemiplimab for patients with metastatic cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) or locally advanced CSCC in patients who are not a candidate for curative surgery or curative dose radiation therapy following a New England Journal of Medicine publication that demonstrated its efficacy in these patient populations. Migden et al. (N Eng J Med 2018) completed and reported on a phase 1 study of cemiplimab in patients with locally advanced or metastatic CSCC and the pivotal phase 2 study of patients with metastatic disease. In both phases, patients received intravenous cemiplimab (3 mg/kg bodyweight) every 2 weeks and were assessed every 8 weeks for response. With a median follow-up of 7.8 months in the phase 2 portion of the study, they reported the following: The overall response rate in the phase 1 portion of the study was 50% (13 of 26 patients) The overall response rate in the phase 2 portion of the study was 47% (28 of 59 patients) Of the patients who had a response in the phase 2 portion (n=28), 16 had a duration of response that exceeded 6 months (57%). Of the patients who had a response in the phase 2 portion (n=28), 23 continued to have a response to the drug at the time of data cutoff (82%) Common toxicities included diarrhea (27%), fatigue (24%), nausea (17%), constipation (15%), and rash (15%) Overall, 7% of patients discontinued treatment due to toxicity. However, the following patients were EXCLUDED from the trial: Those with autoimmune disease that was treated with systemic immunosuppressive therapy (currently or within last 5 years) Those with autoimmune disease previously treated with anti–PD-1 or anti–programmed death ligand 1 therapy Those who had undergone solid-organ transplantation Those who had concurrent cancer, unless the disease was indolent or was not considered to be life-threatening (e.g., basal-cell carcinoma) Thus, Cemiplimab is generally NOT offered as management option to patients with CSCC on immunosuppression related to organ transplantation. @Neet_pg_bot

Cemiplimab is a potent, high-affinity human monoclonal antibody directed against programmed death 1 (PD-1). It is used in the management of lung cancer, multiple myeloma, and squamous cell carcinoma of the skin. PD-1 is expressed on the surface of activated T-cells, B-cells, and myeloid cells. When programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) binds to PD-1, it delivers a signal to inhibit T-cell proliferation. By binding to PD-1, pembrolizumab prevents tumour cell PD-L1 from binding to it, allowing the immune system to target and destroy the malignant cells. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved cemiplimab for patients with metastatic cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) or locally advanced CSCC in patients who are not a candidate for curative surgery or curative dose radiation therapy following a New England Journal of Medicine publication that demonstrated its efficacy in these patient populations.

Migden et al. (N Eng J Med 2018) completed and reported on a phase 1 study of cemiplimab in patients with locally advanced or metastatic CSCC and the pivotal phase 2 study of patients with metastatic disease. In both phases, patients received intravenous cemiplimab (3 mg/kg bodyweight) every 2 weeks and were assessed every 8 weeks for response. With a median follow-up of 7.8 months in the phase 2 portion of the study, they reported the following:

  • The overall response rate in the phase 1 portion of the study was 50% (13 of 26 patients)
  • The overall response rate in the phase 2 portion of the study was 47% (28 of 59 patients)
  • Of the patients who had a response in the phase 2 portion (n=28), 16 had a duration of response that exceeded 6 months (57%).
  • Of the patients who had a response in the phase 2 portion (n=28), 23 continued to have a response to the drug at the time of data cutoff (82%)
  • Common toxicities included diarrhea (27%), fatigue (24%), nausea (17%), constipation (15%), and rash (15%)
  • Overall, 7% of patients discontinued treatment due to toxicity.

However, the following patients were EXCLUDED from the trial:

  • Those with autoimmune disease that was treated with systemic immunosuppressive therapy (currently or within last 5 years)
  • Those with autoimmune disease previously treated with anti–PD-1 or anti–programmed death ligand 1 therapy
  • Those who had undergone solid-organ transplantation
  • Those who had concurrent cancer, unless the disease was indolent or was not considered to be life-threatening (e.g., basal-cell carcinoma)

Thus, Cemiplimab is generally NOT offered as management option to patients with CSCC on immunosuppression related to organ transplantation.

questions.solution: Correct Option B - olanzapine: The medication that is least likely to have precipitated the patient's symptoms is olanzapine. The patient presents with fever, agitation, dilated pupils, tremors, hyperreflexia, and clonus, which are suggestive of serotonin syndrome. Serotonin syndrome is a potentially life-threatening condition that can occur when there is an excess of serotonin in the central nervous system. It is often associated with the use of serotonergic medications or the combination of multiple serotonergic drugs. Olanzapine is an atypical antipsychotic medication. While it does have some serotonergic activity, it is not typically considered a primary precipitant of serotonin syndrome. It is less likely to be the cause in this case. It can potentially contribute to serotonin syndrome, especially when used in combination with other serotonergic drugs. It can increase serotonin levels and is associated with the risk of serotonin syndrome, especially when used inappropriately or in combination with other serotonergic drugs. questions.stem: A 1-day-old infant is diagnosed with D-transposition of the great arteries. He is admitted to intensive care and receives a balloon atrial septostomy to ensure adequate atrial level shunting. The patient undergoes an arterial switch procedure at 4 days of age and does well postoperatively. Why is early surgery preferable to waiting several months before operating?
questions.stemHtml: A 1-day-old infant is diagnosed with D-transposition of the great arteries. He is admitted to intensive care and receives a balloon atrial septostomy to ensure adequate atrial level shunting. The patient undergoes an arterial switch procedure at 4 days of age and does well postoperatively. Why is early surgery preferable to waiting several months before operating?

options.label: A
options.text: It takes advantage of the low pulmonary pressure in the newborn period.

options.label: B
options.text: It takes advantage of high systemic pressures in the newborn period.

options.label: C
options.text: It allows early connection of the coronary arteries to the pulmonary artery.

options.label: D
options.text: It retains left ventricular mass so that it can perform normally when attached to the systemic circulation.

questions.answerText: It retains left ventricular mass so that it can perform normally when attached to the systemic circulation.
questions.solution: Correct Option D - It retains left ventricular mass so that it can perform normally when attached to the systemic circulation: The anomaly of d-transposition of the great arteries (TGA) involves the attachment of the ventricles to the wrong great arteries. The right ventricle is connected to the aorta, while the left ventricle connects to the pulmonary artery. The coronary arteries always arise from the aorta, hence with TGA the coronaries receive deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle. An anatomic (complete) correction moves the coronary arteries and great arteries back to their normal positions. This arterial switch must be done early, while the left ventricle still retains a normal mass. If surgery is delayed, the left ventricle may atrophy due to its pumping into the low-resistance pulmonary circulation. Incorrect Options: Option A - It takes advantage of the low pulmonary pressure in the newborn period: Pulmonary pressures fall following delivery, but continue to decline for weeks thereafter. This is not the reason for the decision to operate early. Option B - It takes advantage of high systemic pressures in the newborn period: Systemic blood pressures in the early newborn period are not typically elevated. Option C - It allows early connection of the coronary arteries to the pulmonary artery: Coronary arteries must remain connected to the aorta. They will receive fully oxygenated blood once the aorta is connected to the left ventricle. @Neet_pg_bot

An anatomic (complete) correction moves the coronary arteries and great arteries back to their normal positions. This arterial switch must be done early, while the left ventricle still retains a normal mass. If surgery is delayed, the left ventricle may atrophy due to its pumping into the low-resistance pulmonary circulation.

 

Incorrect Options:

Option A -  It takes advantage of the low pulmonary pressure in the newborn period: Pulmonary pressures fall following delivery, but continue to decline for weeks thereafter. This is not the reason for the decision to operate early.

Option B - It takes advantage of high systemic pressures in the newborn period: Systemic blood pressures in the early newborn period are not typically elevated.

questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old female patient presents for evaluation of fecal incontinence. She has been involuntarily soiling her clothes and is now afraid to leave her home as a result.
