questions.solution: Correct Option B - Endoanal ultrasound TRUE - The patient has passive incontinence, which is characterized by a lack of awareness of the need for defecation prior to having an episode of incontinence. Normally, progressive distension of the rectum leads to a reflex relaxation of the internal anal sphincter. With the increase of stool in the rectum, the urge to defecate increases. During voluntary defecation, there is voluntary straightening of the anorectal angle with increased abdominal pressure from straining. The pelvic floor descends, the rectum contracts, and the external anal sphincter is relaxed, allowing expulsion of rectal contents. The internal anal sphincter undergoes tonic contractions and maintains up to 85% of the anal canal resting pressure, although this is not essential for continence. The endoanal ultrasound can best visualize the internal sphincter. Incorrect Options: Option A -MRI defecography: FALSE- MRI defecography provides clear images of the soft tissue around the rectum and anal canal. The IAS is better visualized with endoanal ultrasound. Option C - Sigmoidoscopy: FALSE - Flexible sigmoidoscopy is often performed in younger patients to exclude masses or mucosal inflammation as the etiology of incontinence. Option D - Balloon expulsion test: FALSE - The balloon expulsion test is used to identify dyssynergic defecation in patients with fecal impaction and overflow incontinence. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old female patient complains of abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea of 1 day duration, and a cough. She has rheumatoid arthritis and recently began treatment with adalimumab. Her temperature is 101.8°F, and the physical exam is significant for diffuse petechiae and bilateral wheezes on auscultation of the chest. Her WBC count is 12,800 with 13% eosinophils. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral infiltrates, and abdominal CT reveals thickening throughout the ascending colon. Which of the following medications is indicated in addition to broad-spectrum antibiotics?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Ivermectin: This patient’s presentation suggests a hyperinfection syndrome due to Strongyloides stercoralis infection, triggered when she began treatment for her RA with an anti-tumor necrosis factor medication. Hyperinfection is generally due to depressed host cellular immunity. The rhabditiform larvae penetrate the intestinal wall and enter the bloodstream after transforming into filariform larvae. questions.stem: A 38-year-old female is being treated for atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT). Since this is tachyarrhythmia caused by a reentry phenomenon, which mechanism of action could a drug possess that would effectively treat this arrhythmia?
questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old female is being treated for atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT). Since this is tachyarrhythmia caused by a reentry phenomenon, which mechanism of action could a drug possess that would effectively treat this arrhythmia?

options.label: B
options.text: Improves cardiac electrical conduction and decreases cardiac electrical conduction

questions.solution: AVNRT is a type of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) characterized by a reentry circuit within the atrioventricular (AV) node. In AVNRT, an abnormal pathway or circuit allows electrical impulses to continuously circle within the AV node, leading to a rapid heart rate. To treat AVNRT effectively, you want to slow down or block the abnormal electrical conduction within the AV node. This helps to break the reentrant circuit and restore a normal heart rate. Drugs that decrease cardiac electrical conduction, specifically within the AV node, are often used to treat AVNRT. These drugs include: Adenosine: Adenosine is a common choice for acute termination of AVNRT. It decreases conduction through the AV node and can briefly interrupt the reentrant circuit, leading to a transient pause in the arrhythmia. Beta-Blockers: Beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol, propranolol) slow down electrical conduction through the AV node by blocking the effects of adrenaline. This helps prevent and control episodes of AVNRT. Calcium Channel Blockers: Calcium channel blockers (e.g., verapamil, diltiazem) also slow conduction through the AV node, making them useful in preventing and managing AVNRT. In summary, drugs that decrease cardiac electrical conduction within the AV node are effective in treating AVNRT by interrupting the reentrant circuit and restoring normal rhythm. These drugs are commonly used as part of the therapeutic approach for patients with this tachyarrhythmia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Emergent cardiac surgery: The images demonstrate cardiac tamponade. Findings include significant respiratory variation of MV inflows (>25%) and RV diastolic collapse, RA inversion, and inferior vena cava plethora (dilated >2 cm and not collapsing normally with inspiration). A patient with a type I dissection and cardiac tamponade needs to have emergent cardiac surgery as soon as possible for drainage of the pericardium and repair of the aorta. Pericardiocentesis could prompt complete rupture of the flap into the pericardium, causing cardiac arrest and death. An aortic stent graft is currently not the treatment of choice for a type I dissection and could not address the problem of tamponade. Coronary angiography in this patient would only delay the definitive therapy (surgery) as well as possibly further propagate the dissection flap. Delay of surgery in a patient with a type I dissection is associated with a 1% per hour increase in mortality in the first 48 hours of the process. (Note that this patient has not had prior cardiac surgery; if the person had prior cardiac surgery, it would likely change the need for cardiac catheterization prior to surgery.) @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: What is the RBC antigen most commonly associated with paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria?
questions.stemHtml: What is the RBC antigen most commonly associated with paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - P antigen Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria (PCH) is an autoimmune haemolytic anaemia associated with a polyclonal IgG targeted to the P antigen causing intravascular haemolysis through complement fixation. It is most common in children but can present in adults as well. Often times associated with a post viral infection presentation with dark urine upon exposure to cold. Typically patients will have a positive DAT for C3 and negative for IgG. Cold agglutinin titre is typically low as compared to cold agglutinin disease and the diagnostic test is the Donath-Landsteiner reaction, in which the patient's serum is cooled to 4 degrees C with normal red blood cells and then rewarmed to 37 degrees C to allow for late complement fixation and lysis. (Shanbhag et al. Haematology Oncology Clinics of North America. 2015) Incorrect Options: Option A - i/I antigen: The i/I antigen system is most commonly implicated in cold agglutinin disease both in virally associated presentations as well as IgM monoclonal antibody or lymphoma associated presentations. Option B - Duffy antigen group: The Duffy antigen is a chemokine receptor that is the target for certain malarial infections as well as implicated in antibody mediated reactions causing haemolytic transfusion reactions and haemolytic disease of the new-born. Option D - Kell antigen group: The Kell antigen system is implicated (antibodies to Kell antigens) in haemolytic transfusion reactions and is a rare target in warm haemolytic anaemias. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option C - P antigen

  • Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria (PCH) is an autoimmune haemolytic anaemia associated with a polyclonal IgG targeted to the P antigen causing intravascular haemolysis through complement fixation. It is most common in children but can present in adults as well.
  • Often times associated with a post viral infection presentation with dark urine upon exposure to cold. Typically patients will have a positive DAT for C3 and negative for IgG. Cold agglutinin titre is typically low as compared to cold agglutinin disease and the diagnostic test is the Donath-Landsteiner reaction, in which the patient's serum is cooled to 4 degrees C with normal red blood cells and then rewarmed to 37 degrees C to allow for late complement fixation and lysis. (Shanbhag et al. Haematology Oncology Clinics of North America. 2015)

Incorrect Options: 

Option A - i/I antigen: The i/I antigen system is most commonly implicated in cold agglutinin disease both in virally associated presentations as well as IgM monoclonal antibody or lymphoma associated presentations.

Option B - Duffy antigen group: The Duffy antigen is a chemokine receptor that is the target for certain malarial infections as well as implicated in antibody mediated reactions causing haemolytic transfusion reactions and haemolytic disease of the new-born.

Option D - Kell antigen group: The Kell antigen system is implicated (antibodies to Kell antigens) in haemolytic transfusion reactions and is a rare target in warm haemolytic anaemias.

questions.answerText: Decreased arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2)
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Decreased arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2): This patient is likely experiencing a panic attack, which usually involves the sudden onset of shortness of breath, palpitations, sweating, and an intense fear of dying. The rapid breathing during an attack can result in hyperventilation, which decreases arterial PaCO2 (hypocapnia). Hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction and decreased cerebral perfusion. This results in neurological symptoms like dizziness, weakness, and blurred vision. Whereas hypocapnia reduces cerebral perfusion, hypercapnia increases perfusion via cerebral vasodilation. Cerebral blood flow is directly proportional to PaCO2 until values exceed 90 mmHg when flow becomes constant. Cerebral perfusion is also affected by hypoxia to a lesser degree, and a decrease in PaO2 below 50 mmHg will result in an increase in cerebral blood flow. Incorrect Options: Option A - Decreased arterial total oxygen content: Arterial oxygen content does not decrease with hyperventilation. Option C - Decreased arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2): Arterial PaO2 does not decrease with hyperventilation. Option D - Increased alveolar-arterial O2 gradient: The alveolar-arterial O2 gradient does not change significantly with hyperventilation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: > Seizure disorder. Explanation: Neurocardiogenic (vasovagal) syncope: While vasovagal syncope can cause transient loss of consciousness, it typically presents with a prodrome such as nausea, lightheadedness, or diaphoresis before the loss of consciousness. This patient had no prodrome and experienced upper extremity twitching, which is not a characteristic feature of vasovagal syncope. Seizure disorder: The witnessed transient loss of consciousness, especially with associated upper extremity twitching, is highly suggestive of a seizure episode. The ECG findings of right atrial enlargement with prominent P waves, first-degree atrioventricular block, and right bundle branch block are likely related to his underlying Ebstein anomaly and not directly causative of the seizure. Ventricular tachycardia: Ventricular tachycardia is less likely in this case because the ECG demonstrates sinus rhythm with right atrial enlargement and atrioventricular block, which are not typical findings in ventricular tachycardia. Atrioventricular re-entrant (accessory pathway) tachycardia: Atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia involving an accessory pathway can cause rapid heart rhythms, but it would not explain the witnessed loss of consciousness and upper extremity twitching, which are more indicative of a seizure. In summary, given the patient's symptoms, witnessed loss of consciousness, and associated upper extremity twitching, a seizure disorder is the most likely explanation. questions.stem: A 34-year-old female came to the clinic with complaints of nausea, vomiting, and sudden onset severe right-sided flank pain radiating to the groin for the last 7 days. The pain is not associated with fever and chills, but she has reported urinary frequency and urgency. She is a smoker and has not been sexually active. Urine pregnancy test is negative. She has had ulcerative colitis for the last 6 years and is taking sulfasalazine and steroids. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the pain?
questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old female came to the clinic with complaints of nausea, vomiting, and sudden onset severe right-sided flank pain radiating to the groin for the last 7 days. The pain is not associated with fever and chills, but she has reported urinary frequency and urgency. She is a smoker and has not been sexually active. Urine pregnancy test is negative. She has had ulcerative colitis for the last 6 years and is taking sulfasalazine and steroids. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the pain?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Calcium oxalate stones This patient has developed sudden onset severe unilateral flank pain, nausea, and vomiting with underlying inflammatory bowel disease, most likely suggesting that she has calcium oxalate stones. Calcium oxalate is the most common stone. The underlying etiologies include hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, vitamin C abuse, and ethylene glycol poisoning. In ulcerative colitis, there is fat malabsorption leading to increased fatty acids. Calcium binds these fatty acids, resulting in increased levels of free oxalate, increasing oxalate absorption from the intestine. Most calculi originate within the kidney and proceed distally, creating various degrees of urinary obstruction as they become lodged in narrow areas. The location and quality of pain are related to the position of the stone within the urinary tract. The severity of pain is related to the degree of obstruction, presence of ureteral spasm, and presence of any associated infection. Urine microscopy will reveal octahedron-shaped crystals. These stones are radio-opaque in nature, so these stones are visible on an X-ray or CT scan. Incorrect Options: Option A - Ectopic pregnancy Patients with ectopic pregnancy can present with nausea, vomiting, and unilateral flank pain. In ectopic pregnancy, the patient may present with hemodynamic instability. This is less likely in this patient as she is not sexually active. Option B - Ovarian torsion Ovarian torsion can present with sudden abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. It usually occurs after physical activity and is common in patients with ovarian cysts or masses. The pain of ovarian torsion is dull and continuous and it does not radiate to the groin. Option D - Struvite stones These stones occur after urinary tract infection by urease-positive organisms, i.e. Proteus mirabilis and Klebsiella. These stones are large and block the renal papillae. These are not formed in patients with ulcerative colitis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Hydralazine-isosorbide: The current ACC AHA guidelines recommend hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate given data supporting improved survival with HFrEF who are already on a beta-blocker and ACEi. questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presented in OPD with the complaint of recurrent urinary tract infections. Investigation shows grade III vesicoureteral reflux. What is the single best step in the management of this child?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-year-old child presented in OPD with the complaint of recurrent urinary tract infections. Investigation shows grade III vesicoureteral reflux. What is the single best step in the management of this child?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Reimplantation of ureters Vesicoureteral reflux is the retrograde urine flow in 35% of patients with urinary tract infections. It increases the risk of pyelonephritis. It is classified into five grades based on the appearance of the urinary tract on a contrast micturating cystourethrogram. Grades of vesicoureteral reflux Grade I Reflux into a non-dilated ureter Grade II Reflux into the upper collecting system without dilatation. Grade III Reflux into the dilated ureter and blunting of calyceal fornices. Grade IV Reflux into the kidney and grossly dilated ureter. Grade V Massive reflux into the kidney, with ureteral dilatation and tortuosity and effacement of calyceal details. The risk of recurrent UTI is highly associated with grade III and IV VUR. The most important and definitive treatment is surgery involving the reimplantation of ureters. As normally, there is an oblique insertion of ureters. Therefore, surgery involves the modification of abnormal ureterovesical attachment. The success rate of open ureters reimplantation is >95-98%. Incorrect Options: Option B - Urine culture It is carried out in the investigation of urinary tract infection, and the presence of a count of 10⁵ colony forming units/ml for a single organism is considered an infected case. Option C - Antimicrobial prophylaxis Antimicrobial prophylaxis is given as it decreases the risk of recurrent urinary tract infections in vesicoureteral reflux. However, it may increase the risk of developing resistant bacteria. Option D - Behavioral modification These include timed voiding, increased fluid intake, periodic assessment of bladder emptying, and prompt UTI assessment and treatment. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option A - Reimplantation of ureters

  • Vesicoureteral reflux is the retrograde urine flow in 35% of patients with urinary tract infections.
  • It increases the risk of pyelonephritis.
  • It is classified into five grades based on the appearance of the urinary tract on a contrast micturating cystourethrogram.
  • Grades of vesicoureteral reflux
  • Grade I
    • Reflux into a non-dilated ureter
  • Grade II
    • Reflux into the upper collecting system without dilatation.
  • Grade III
    • Reflux into the dilated ureter and blunting of calyceal fornices.
  • Grade IV
    • Reflux into the kidney and grossly dilated ureter.
  • Grade V
    • Massive reflux into the kidney, with ureteral dilatation and tortuosity and effacement of calyceal details.
  • The risk of recurrent UTI is highly associated with grade III and IV VUR.
  • The most important and definitive treatment is surgery involving the reimplantation of ureters.
  • As normally, there is an oblique insertion of ureters. Therefore, surgery involves the modification of abnormal ureterovesical attachment.
  • The success rate of open ureters reimplantation is >95-98%.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Urine culture

  • It is carried out in the investigation of urinary tract infection, and the presence of a count of 10⁵ colony forming units/ml for a single organism is considered an infected case.

Option C - Antimicrobial prophylaxis

  • Antimicrobial prophylaxis is given as it decreases the risk of recurrent urinary tract infections in vesicoureteral reflux.
  • However, it may increase the risk of developing resistant bacteria.

Option D - Behavioral modification

  • These include timed voiding, increased fluid intake, periodic assessment of bladder emptying, and prompt UTI assessment and treatment.

He continues to have angina with moderate aerobic exercise that is completely relieved by 1 sublingual nitroglycerin. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Atherosclerotic epicardial coronary artery obstruction: Myocardial ischemia is determined by the balance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand. Myocardial oxygen demand is determined by heart rate, myocardial contractility, and myocardial wall tension. A normal oxygen supply to the myocardium requires adequate inspired oxygen, intact lung function, normal hemoglobin concentration, and normal coronary blood flow. Resistance to coronary blood flow is determined by 3 vascular regions: large epicardial arteries, peri-arteriolar vessels, and intra-myocardial capillaries. The most common pathophysiologic mechanism causing stable ischemic heart disease is atherosclerotic epicardial coronary artery obstruction. However, as many as one-third of patients may have no significant epicardial disease and often have microvascular disease as the underlying pathophysiology. Incorrect Options: Option B - Coronary microvascular dysfunction: Coronary microvascular dysfunction refers to the pathology affecting smaller coronary arteries (by convention, those less than 500 micrometers). These are pre-arterioles and arterioles that feed the capillaries and regulate myocardial blood flow. It is a much less common cause of stable ischemic heart disease than atherosclerotic epicardial coronary artery obstruction. Option C - Vasospastic angina: Vasospastic angina is a clinical entity characterized by episodes of rest angina that promptly respond to short-acting nitrates and are attributable to coronary artery vasospasm. This condition is a much less common cause of stable ischemic heart disease than atherosclerotic epicardial coronary artery obstruction. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by his son after he found him lying on the ground. The patient is unable to speak and is unable to walk properly. Physical examination reveals an irregular pulse, weakness of the left upper and lower extremities, and aphasia. His medical history is significant for diabetes, COPD and hypertension all of which are well-controlled by medications. An ECG is performed and shown below. Which of the following interventions could have prevented this patient’s condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by his son after he found him lying on the ground. The patient is unable to speak and is unable to walk properly. Physical examination reveals an irregular pulse, weakness of the left upper and lower extremities, and aphasia. His medical history is significant for diabetes, COPD and hypertension all of which are well-controlled by medications. An ECG is performed and shown below. Which of the following interventions could have prevented this patient’s condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Prophylactic anticoagulation: This patient with acute onset left-sided weakness and aphasia is most likely suffering from a stroke, particularly an embolic stroke in light of this patient’s underlying atrial fibrillation as proven by the ECG findings. Pathogenesis of A-fib is characterized by abnormal automatic firing and the presence of multiple interacting reentry circuits looping around the atria. Episodes of AF are initiated by rapid bursts of ectopic beats arising from conducting tissue in the pulmonary veins or from diseased/dilated atrial tissue. Atrial fibrillation most commonly occurs due to atrial remodeling as a result of hypertension (as in this patient) and other cardiac disorders e.g. mitral stenosis. Atrial fibrillation results in stasis of blood flow in the left atrium . As a result, there is an increased risk of thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage. This thrombus can subsequently embolize into the systemic circulation and lead to ischemia of the affected region. The risk of thrombosis can be reduced by the use of anticoagulation that prevents the formation of clots that eventually lodge in the distal circulation. Incorrect Options: Option A - Synchronized cardioversion: This treatment modality is used to terminate atrial fibrillation that leads to hemodynamic instability i.e. hypotension. It cannot mitigate the risk of thrombosis. Option C - Defibrillation: This intervention is used to terminate ventricular fibrillation It has no role in A-fib Option D - Angioplasty: Angioplasty is done in cases of myocardial infarction which presents as chest pain radiating to the neck and left arm, diaphoresis, and an impending sense of doom. An MI presents with ST-elevations on ECG @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option B - Prophylactic anticoagulation:

  • Pathogenesis of A-fib is characterized by abnormal automatic firing and the presence of multiple interacting reentry circuits looping around the atria. Episodes of AF are initiated by rapid bursts of ectopic beats arising from conducting tissue in the pulmonary veins or from diseased/dilated atrial tissue.
  • Atrial fibrillation most commonly occurs due to atrial remodeling as a result of hypertension (as in this patient) and other cardiac disorders e.g. mitral stenosis.
  • Atrial fibrillation results in stasis of blood flow in the left atrium. As a result, there is an increased risk of thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage.
  • This thrombus can subsequently embolize into the systemic circulation and lead to ischemia of the affected region.
  • The risk of thrombosis can be reduced by the use of anticoagulation that prevents the formation of clots that eventually lodge in the distal circulation.

 

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Synchronized cardioversion:

  • This treatment modality is used to terminate atrial fibrillation that leads to hemodynamic instability i.e. hypotension.
  • It cannot mitigate the risk of thrombosis.

Option C - Defibrillation:

  • This intervention is used to terminate ventricular fibrillation
  • It has no role in A-fib

questions.stem: A 28-year-old female patient comes to the clinic with complaints of cough, wheezing, and shortness of breath after exercising. She denies any similar symptoms at rest or any other known allergies or medical conditions. What is the mechanism behind exercise-induced asthma?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old female patient comes to the clinic with complaints of cough, wheezing, and shortness of breath after exercising. She denies any similar symptoms at rest or any other known allergies or medical conditions. What is the mechanism behind exercise-induced asthma?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased airway resistance due to bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy

options.label: B
options.text: Airway narrowing due to inflammation and oedema of the airway epithelium

options.label: C
options.text: Increased airway resistance due to a decrease in surfactant production

options.label: D
options.text: Airway obstruction due to mucus hypersecretion

questions.answerText: Airway narrowing due to inflammation and oedema of the airway epithelium
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Airway narrowing due to inflammation and oedema of the airway epithelium Exercise-induced asthma (EIA), also known as exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB), is a type of asthma triggered by physical activity. During exercise, increased ventilation and airway cooling can cause the airways to narrow, leading to symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. The exact mechanism behind EIA is not fully understood, but it is thought to be related to the release of inflammatory mediators such as histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins from mast cells and other cells in the airways. These mediators cause bronchoconstriction and inflammation in the airways, leading to the symptoms of EIA. Management of EIA involves avoiding triggers and using medications to prevent symptoms. Pre-exercise use of a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) inhaler, such as albuterol, can help prevent symptoms in many cases. In addition, warming up before exercise, exercising in warm and humid environments, and wearing a face mask or scarf over the mouth and nose can also help reduce symptoms. Incorrect Options: Option A - Increased airway resistance due to bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy This is a mechanism of chronic asthma and not specific to exercise-induced asthma. Option C - Increased airway resistance due to a decrease in surfactant production Surfactant is a substance that reduces surface tension within the alveoli and helps prevent them from collapsing. It is not directly related to the pathophysiology of exercise-induced asthma. Option D - Airway obstruction due to mucus hypersecretion Mucus hypersecretion is a feature of chronic bronchitis, but it is not a prominent feature of exercise-induced asthma. @Neet_pg_bot

One to two times per week he will go to sleep in his bed and wake up in a different part of the house with no recollection of how he got there. Which of the following characteristics would favor a diagnosis of a NREM parasomnia over nocturnal seizures?

A 19 year-old man presents for evaluation of abnormal behaviors in sleep. One to two times per week he will go to sleep in his bed and wake up in a different part of the house with no recollection of how he got there.

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Distinct onset and offset: The characteristic that would favor a diagnosis of a NREM (Non-Rapid Eye Movement) parasomnia over nocturnal seizures in this case is: NREM parasomnias and nocturnal seizures can sometimes have overlapping symptoms, such as unusual behaviors during sleep, but there are key differences between the two. NREM parasomnias often have a more distinct and gradual onset and offset, meaning the episodes start and end more gradually. In contrast, seizures, including nocturnal seizures, often have a more abrupt and less gradual onset and offset. A person with NREM parasomnia may transition in and out of the episode more smoothly, while someone with a seizure may have more abrupt and less predictable transitions. Incorrect Options: Option A - Stereotyped events: Both NREM parasomnias and nocturnal seizures can involve stereotyped events, meaning the episodes have a consistent and repetitive pattern. This is a feature common to both conditions and does not help differentiate between them. Option C - Long duration (greater than 5 minutes): Both NREM parasomnias and seizures can have long durations, so this feature is not specific to either condition. Option D - Multiple episodes in one night: Both conditions can result in multiple episodes in one night, so this feature does not provide a clear distinction. Option E - Exacerbation by sleep deprivation: Both NREM parasomnias and seizures can be exacerbated by sleep deprivation, so this feature is not specific to one condition over the other. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Chronic alcohol abuse: A known risk factor for the onset of myocarditis is chronic alcohol usage. Alcohol can have toxic effects on the heart muscle, which can result in inflammation and cell damage. Chronic alcohol misuse can also impair immunity, leaving the body more vulnerable to illnesses resulting in myocarditis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hypertension: A chronic illness known as hypertension causes higher arterial blood pressure. Although many cardiovascular disorders, such as coronary artery disease and heart failure, are at increased risk due to hypertension, myocarditis is not one of them. Option B - Hyperlipidemia: Although hyperlipidemia is not a known risk factor for myocarditis, it is a risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Option D - Diabetes Mellitus: A chronic metabolic condition called diabetes mellitus is characterized by elevated blood sugar levels. Diabetes is an established risk factor for coronary artery disease and heart failure, among other cardiovascular disorders, but it is not one for myocarditis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Loud S2 Pulmonary arterial hypertension occurs in about 12% of patients with limited systemic sclerosis due to obliterative vascular disease. Patients are most commonly asymptomatic but may present with dyspnoea, syncope and chest (anginal) pain. A right ventricular heave occurs where there is right ventricular hypertrophy and this creates an 'a' wave in the neck veins. This accelerates the right heart failure with worsening peripheral oedema and pulsatile swelling of the liver. questions.stem: A patient with severe hemophilia A, with recent numerous admissions during the last 2.5 years, for spontaneous bleeding in the soft tissues and joints, but no arthropathy, seeks your opinion, on treatment to prevent any future bleeds. He has never required a bypass agent. What would you recommend?
questions.stemHtml: A patient with severe hemophilia A, with recent numerous admissions during the last 2.5 years, for spontaneous bleeding in the soft tissues and joints, but no arthropathy, seeks your opinion, on treatment to prevent any future bleeds. He has never required a bypass agent. What would you recommend?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Emicizumab: For a patient with severe hemophilia A who has a history of frequent spontaneous bleeding in the absence of arthropathy and has not required a bypass agent, the most appropriate and recommended treatment to prevent future bleeds is Emicizumab. Emicizumab is a bispecific monoclonal antibody that mimics the function of factor VIII in the coagulation cascade. It is used for the prophylactic treatment of bleeding in patients with hemophilia A, including those with factor VIII inhibitors. Emicizumab is administered subcutaneously and is effective in preventing both spontaneous and provoked bleeds. It is a convenient and effective option for prophylactic treatment, even in patients who have a history of frequent bleeding episodes. Incorrect Options: Option B - Recombinant Factor VIII 3x Weekly: Recombinant factor VIII replacement therapy is a traditional treatment for hemophilia A. However, frequent infusions of factor VIII three times a week may not be as effective in preventing bleeds as emicizumab, and it can be more burdensome for the patient. Option C - Plasma Derived Factor VIII 3x Weekly: Plasma-derived factor VIII is another traditional treatment option for hemophilia A. Similar to recombinant factor VIII, frequent infusions three times a week may not provide the same level of bleed prevention as emicizumab, and it may require more frequent visits for factor replacement. Option D - Cryoprecipitate 2x Weekly: Cryoprecipitate is not a suitable prophylactic treatment for hemophilia A. It contains various clotting factors, including fibrinogen and factor VIII, but it lacks the precision and convenience of recombinant factor VIII or emicizumab. @Neet_pg_bot

Calcium: 9.5 mg/dL

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Surgical resection followed by radiation: The recommended treatment for this patient with a well-defined lytic lesion in the C5 vertebral body and evidence of clonal plasma cells on biopsy, especially in the absence of other multiple myeloma-related findings, is Surgical resection followed by radiation. This is the recommended approach for solitary plasmacytoma of bone. Surgical resection aims to remove the affected bone and any nearby tissue with clonal plasma cells. After surgery, radiation therapy is administered to the surgical bed to further eliminate any remaining cancer cells and reduce the risk of local recurrence. This combined approach has been shown to provide good local control and improve long-term outcomes in patients with SPB. Incorrect Options: Option A - Radiation therapy alone: Radiation therapy alone may provide symptomatic relief, but it is not typically curative for solitary plasmacytoma of bone (SPB). SPB is a localized form of plasma cell dyscrasia that affects a single bone. While radiation therapy can be used to manage pain and control the local disease, it is often followed by surgical resection in patients who are good candidates for surgery. Option C - Surgery alone: Surgery alone may be considered in certain cases, but it is usually followed by radiation therapy. Surgical resection can help remove the affected bone and any surrounding tissue that may contain clonal plasma cells. However, radiation therapy is often recommended to target any residual disease and reduce the risk of recurrence. Option D - Chemotherapy and/or bone marrow transplant: In cases where multiple myeloma is confirmed or strongly suspected, chemotherapy and/or bone marrow transplant may be considered. However, in this patient's scenario, there is no evidence of multiple myeloma based on the laboratory and imaging findings. Therefore, aggressive multiple myeloma treatment is not warranted. In summary, for a patient with a solitary plasmacytoma of bone, the preferred treatment strategy is Surgical resection followed by radiation therapy to achieve local control and potentially cure the disease while preserving spinal function and reducing the risk of recurrence. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A three-year-old girl is referred to you for evaluation of several months of progressive gait issues. There is no abnormality on the skin examination over her lumbosacral spine, but imaging reveals a low-lying conus medullaris, consistent with tethered cord syndrome. Thickening of which structure is responsible for tethered cord syndrome?
questions.stemHtml:
A three-year-old girl is referred to you for evaluation of several months of progressive gait issues. There is no abnormality on the skin examination over her lumbosacral spine, but imaging reveals a low-lying conus medullaris, consistent with tethered cord syndrome.
Thickening of which structure is responsible for tethered cord syndrome?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Filum terminale Tethered cord syndrome is a neurological disorder where the spinal cord becomes abnormally attached to the surrounding tissues, typically due to an abnormal thickening or scarring of the filum terminale. The filum terminale is a delicate fibrous band that extends from the tip of the conus medullaris (the lower end of the spinal cord) to the coccyx (tailbone). When the filum terminale thickens and becomes less elastic, it can exert abnormal tension on the spinal cord, leading to various neurological symptoms, including progressive gait issues, bladder and bowel dysfunction, lower limb weakness, and pain. This abnormal attachment can limit the mobility of the spinal cord and cause traction on the nerve roots. Incorrect Options: Option A - Cauda equina: The cauda equina is a bundle of spinal nerve roots at the lower end of the spinal cord. While compression or injury to the cauda equina can cause neurological symptoms, it is not the primary structure involved in tethered cord syndrome. Option B - Conus medullaris: The conus medullaris is the lower end of the spinal cord, and a low-lying conus medullaris can be a result of tethered cord syndrome, but it is not the structure responsible for the thickening and tethering. Option C - Dura: The dura mater is the outermost membrane covering the spinal cord, and although it plays a protective role, it is not typically the structure responsible for tethered cord syndrome. Option E - Lumbosacral nerve roots: While nerve roots may be affected by the tethered cord, they are not responsible for the thickening or tethering process. @Neet_pg_bot
